en: Having bowed to that stainless [Lord], a concise commentary is composed for the sake of understanding the words in this supreme scripture, *Śivārkamaṇidīpikā*, specifically regarding the section known as the "Vidyāpāda.

For elsewhere, I have already provided an extensive determination of the meaning of the categories (*padārtha*) through reasoning and scripture, intended as a common work to cut away doubts concerning the established doctrine.

It is said that in ancient times, when the Blessed Lord, the husband of Umā, was bestowing his grace upon Garuḍa, a certain disciple or grand-disciple of his related to his own disciples exactly what kind of scripture had been taught and in what form:
"To Soma, who sits upon the peak of Kailāsa, whose crest is the crescent moon..."
Having seen Hara, Tārkṣya spoke these words preceded by praise: KirT_1.1 //
Commentary:

As for the fact that some describe at the very outset the nature of the treatise, its connection, its subject matter, and so forth—doing so in a manner contrary to the sūtras—that is indeed improper, because those matters will be explained by the sūtras themselves.
If it is argued that they must necessarily be stated at the beginning as the cause for engaging with the work, [we reply:]...
For, unlike other treatises, it would be impossible to engage with this work by means of its mere title;
for we shall demonstrate here that from the very moment of approaching the teacher, one must proceed everywhere solely on the basis of the teacher’s word and not otherwise.
In this context, "the peak of Kailāsa" refers to its summit.

By the phrase "seeing him seated there," the distinction of this God—who will be described as situated within the sphere above the worlds of Brahmā and Viṣṇu because he stands in the midst of yogins—is indicated. By the phrase "him who dwells together with Umā," the distinction from Śrī Nandikeśvara and others, who are also seated on the peak of Kailāsa, is shown.

Now, according to the maxim that "conventional usage (rūḍhi) supersedes etymological derivation (yoga)," one might here understand the word *soma* to refer simply to the moon. To preclude this, [the text says] "having seen him whose crest is half of that *soma* upon his head.

Furthermore, he is called *Hara* because he removes (*harati*) the bonds of men and leads them to the state beyond the person; thus the meaning is: "Tārkṣya, having seen his own guru, [the Lord] Hara.
From this very fact, it is understood that his initiation into liberation (*nirvāṇadīkṣā*) has been accomplished.

Since he will state that those who have not received initiation lack the qualification for hearing [the scripture], when the word *hara* is explained by its conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) alone as "the husband of Umā," it would be redundant because there is no other thing to be excluded; therefore, an explanation based on its connection with a specific action is superior.
And here, since the act of seeing is already established by the very force of the act of bowing, the meaning is not "having seen Hara."
Rather, the phrase "having seen preceded by praise" (*stutipūrvam dṛṣṭvā*) should be explained here as an adverbial modifier of the action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*),
and not as a modifier of the speech (*vacoviśeṣaṇa*).

Consequently, the meaning is that Vainateya spoke these words after having propitiated the Blessed One, who was distinguished by the performance of deeds such as the slaying of Andhaka, which were to be described later, and which were characterized by prior praise.
Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever.
Now, as for that praise which was previously mentioned with the words "having seen," it is stated therein:
"O you who are skilled in breaking the bonds of the broad-shouldered Andhaka!"
Victory to you, O Lord of preeminent heroes, who has restrained the consumer of cities!
Victory to you, O terrifying one who severed the heads of all the lords of the gods!
Victory to you, whose power is renowned, the destroyer of the stability of Manmatha!
Victory to you, who destroyed the body of Acyuta and removed the power of the Kālakūṭa poison;
victory to you, who restrained the force of the river during the great turbulence of the whirlpool!
Victory to you, who deluded the wives of the sages in the Dārūvana grove!
Victory to you, who were formidable in the violent agitation of your playful dance!
Victory to you, who terrify the gods and asuras with the fury of your fierce form!
Victory to you, who have displayed magnificent torrents of blood from the mouths of cruel lords of men! KirT_1.6 //
Victory to you, O destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice through the prowess of your heroic strides!
Victory to you, who are proud of the strength of your wondrously great liṅga-form!
Victory to you, O fierce one who brings about the falling of the body of Death through white omens!
Victory to you, O Daughter of the Mountain, who are the abode of all happiness and who delude the god of love!
Victory to you, O dispeller of the darkness of the web of delusion and the fever of suffering!
Victory to you, the burner of the netherworld, the upper worlds, and the world between!
Vṛtti:
Of the great asura Andhaka, there were two broad shoulders; their "bond" was a variegated arrangement, and its "breaking" was the rending apart.
In that regard, you alone are the one who is discerning and wise, and no other.
The address to him is: "O Blessed One who has become thus, victory!
Furthermore, those for whom the excellent boon was granted by Brahmā are the *pravaras*; and those who are heroes are the *vīras*.
O Blessed One, victory to you, the burner of that Tripura which was besieged by those very *pravaravīreśas*!
O Lord, whose head—the head of Brahmā, the ruler of all the gods—was severed in ancient times as described in the Purāṇas and Itihāsas, and who therefore possesses a terrifying and fierce form;

O Destroyer of the body of Manmatha (Kāma), whose power is renowned for deluding the entire triple world, and who is his "sthitih" (abode) because he is the cause of the existence of his [Manmatha's] body and enjoyments; O Blessed One, who also removes the "vega" (force) of the "tanudhvaṃsa" (body-destroyer), namely the Kālakūṭa poison, which was the cause of the destruction of the body of Acyuta (Viṣṇu).
As it is stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa*: "By that poison, as soon as it was manifested, possessing the brilliance of the fire of cosmic destruction..."
"Janārdana, whose limbs were once red and fair, was completely consumed by fire and made black. Thus [it is said in] the Vāyupurāṇa (54:58).
"Balāpaha" means one who seizes away strength; this is an address to him.
Furthermore, an "āvarta" is a whirlpool, and by it, the "mahāṭopa" (great turbulence) is a forceful current; that river—by context, the Jāhnavī—is the "sāvartamahāṭopasarit.
Its "vega" is its force, and the "vidhāraṇa" is the restraining of that.
It is said that such a great river on his head is sustained by the Blessed One alone and by no other; this is a hyperbolic praise. (2–4)

Furthermore, it is the deluder of the wives of those sages who dwell in the hermitage-garden within the forest of *devadāru* trees; for it deludes both the sages—who have not yet conquered desire, anger, and the like—and their wives, due to some particular purpose. In this context, the term has a sense of praise; otherwise, this would be a mere censure, so how could it be a eulogy?
Likewise, there is the play characterized by great exertion consisting of dance, which is the movement of the limbs involving various dramatic gestures (*abhinaya*) and the like.
Due to his extraordinary nature, his sporting consists of the form of the *tāṇḍava* dance.
Through that, there is the agitation and instability of the world; therefore, O Lord, who art fierce and terrifying, conquer!
This is what has been said.
"During whose time of dancing the earth shakes, the mountains split, the oceans stumble, and the sky-dwellers bow down— may that Hara protect us here at the end [of this verse].
Moreover, that fierce and terrifying form of Bhairava, which is described in the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and other texts as being employed to strike fear into Umā— "
He whose fury (*saṃrambha*)—which imitates the dramatic performance (*abhinaya*) characterized by the terror of the world—has terrified the gods and demons; this is his address.
Furthermore, he is addressed as one by whom a truly magnificent torrent of blood was shown as a waterfall upon the mouths of Rāvaṇa, the lord of cruel beings, the Rākṣasas.

Moreover, he is the destroyer of the sacrifice of Dakṣa, the Prajāpati, through the movement—that is, the dispatching—of Vīrabhadra, the hero; O Blessed One, "conquer! is used here for the purpose of praise, otherwise it would be mere censure because of his contemptible nature.

Furthermore, that which is wonderful and marvelous is the Great Liṅga, which pervades the entire triple world; its configuration—that is, its specific form—is composed of flames. Its power is the unbearable intensity of its brilliance. O Blessed One, you who are superior even to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others, and who are proud because of that [power], be victorious! As it has been stated in the Vāyu Purāṇa and other texts:
Suddenly, that wondrous Jvālāliṅga was seen by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the other gods, risen up and pervading all things, both moving and unmoving. (5–7)
Furthermore, [the name] Śveta refers to the Great Sage; "O Blessed One, conquer" refers to the felling of that fierce body of Death for that purpose.

Moreover, Kāma is the abode—that is, the place—of delight in all pleasure; by him Śailajā (Gaurī) was infatuated. Thus, Kāma himself is under his control, or Gaurī, the sovereign of all the worlds, has desire for him.

Furthermore, [the name] Tamohara refers to him who removes the torment of Upamanyu—the exhaustion of the body born of asceticism—as well as the net of delusion, which consists of the fivefold errors and is "tamas" because it functions as darkness. This is his address.

Furthermore: The root of the netherworlds (pātālas) is the realm of the fire of time (kālāgni); above that is the world consisting of sixfold groups of beings, beginning with the immobile and ending with humans.
Non-world (aloka), however, is of a different nature; it consists of the eightfold divine creation, from the Piśācas up to the Pitāmaha (Brahmā).
As it was stated by the Sāṃkhyas:
The divine creation is of eight kinds, and that of the animal realm is fivefold. (Sāṃkhyakārikā 53)
"The human [creation], however, is of one kind; briefly stated, it is the elemental creation.
Thus [it is said]. "The burner of that" is an elliptical expression [for the creator].
O Blessed One, victory to You, the agent of maintenance, protection, bestowal, and grace toward existence!
"Victory! Victory!"—this indeed belongs to this Lord Śrīkaṇṭha by virtue of his authority.

Thus, it is shown that through this hymn consisting of sixteen exploits, there is the vision of this very Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, and not of the Yogins or the Vidyeśvaras who are mentioned in the middle [of the list].

In this way, it is observed that this praise is based on these very exploits alone, and not on other exploits such as the [subduing of] Cakra, Prasāda, the [giving of] half of one’s body, Gaurī, and so forth.
"Andhaka" means blinding darkness; its broad shoulders possess the power to obstruct upward and downward vision. The "bondage" of men by those two is the obstruction of their vision and action.
He who is wise regarding the piercing of that [bondage] by means of initiation—of him is this address.
Thus, they explain that in every respect this praise of the task to be accomplished by initiation here is [to be understood] through a figurative or indirect (lakṣaṇika) mode of expression.
To them, it must be asked: what is the reason for abandoning the well-known meaning and imagining one that is not established here?

For if such were the case without any reason, there would be no distinction between figurative and primary meanings anywhere, and there would be a total failure of comprehension regarding words and sentences. As it has been said:
"Without a purpose, one does not abandon the primary meaning of a word.
[Source: *narte* ... *laṅghanam*]
Source unknown. Also quoted ad *Mātṛkā-vṛtti-prakaraṇa* 3:20 and on p. 12.

In the *Hetubinduṭīkā*, because this hymn concerns Paramaśiva in works such as the *Śrīmadraurava*, and because Paramaśiva is bodiless and thus cannot possess features such as having the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, it is entirely appropriate to postulate a meaning that is not [commonly] established; thus there is no contradiction. //8–9//
Now, what was that speech which Tārkṣya spoke after seeing [the Lord] and having first offered praise? To this it is replied:
"Tell me, who am devoted and afraid, the supreme knowledge of Śiva."
Having attained which, all men go to absolute liberation.
Commentary: One who serves is a *bhakta* (devotee), and one who fears is a *bhīta* (the fearful).

Although his fear of *saṃsāra* has been dispelled by initiation (*dīkṣā*), nevertheless, because it is enjoined by scripture, the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites and so forth must still be performed.
If one fails to perform that [practice] or performs it erroneously, there remains indeed the fear of saṃsāra once again; as it has been said:
"For transgressing the command, the state of being a flesh-eater is proclaimed for a hundred years.
(Ājñā... samāḥ)
There is no fault [in this], as it is attributed by Rāmakaṇṭha in his commentary on Mālinīvijayottara Tantra, Vidyāpāda 5:6 (p. 108) with the expression "in the Pauṣkara and other [tantras]."

And therefore, just as previously you granted me, who was your devotee and filled with fear, the favor known as initiation out of compassion alone, so now please speak the scripture— knowledge which is related to Śiva, the omniscient Lord, both as his manifestation for the sake of the highest good and as that which is to be attained.

By the term "Śiva-knowledge" (śivajñāna), there is an exclusion of the Kaula, Mahāvrata, and other such systems, because they do not have all things as their object and, like the Vaiśeṣika and other schools, were not composed by the Omniscient One.

By the word "supreme" (param), its distinction from the other currents—the Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, Gāruḍa, and Bhūta Tantras—is indicated; for although those too were created by Śiva, they are considered "inferior" because they primarily grant supernatural powers (siddhi).

Now, one might object: "The knowledges of the Vedas and so forth will likewise be 'supreme,' since they were indeed created by the well-known Śivas who are the nature of Hari, Hara, and Hiraṇyagarbha."

That is incorrect, because it is not established that those [teachings] were composed by Śiva, since they teach a liberation whose nature is inauspiciousness (aśivatva). For the impurity of the selves is indeed their inauspiciousness; the absence of that is isolation (kevalitva), which is auspiciousness (śivatā).
Furthermore, they teach that liberation consists in mere impurity (*malakaivalya*), because the nature of impurity is not delimited;

and since that which is undelimited cannot be removed, the prohibition of the Vedas and other scriptures states: "That knowledge, having attained which men reach absolute liberation (*kevalāṃ muktiṃ*)," is likewise [unattainable].
"Crux sarva" (the cross of all),
as it is said by the Blessed One in the *Kiraṇavṛtti*.
Regarding the passage "having attained which all men... [from the *Śivasūtravimarśinī*], Ācārya Rāmakaṇṭha states:
"'All' means Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas... [and so forth]. (See 1:1.11–12).
"Even Vaiśyas, Śūdras, Mlecchas,
and others are indeed qualified by the Śruti; for, starting from the context of Garuḍa’s qualification, the word 'all' (sarva) does not have a restricted meaning."
This has been explained.
(Excerpt from *Śaivāgamādimāhātmya*, IFP T.372, p. 1225, lines 11–16.)
For indeed, Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, Mlecchas,
and others are all entitled to the Vedic revelation;
however, Garuḍa’s entitlement is established because the word "all" (sarva) in the present context has a restricted meaning.
The crux: As it has been said— "The meaning, the context, the indicative mark, and the proximity of another word...
[quote]{arthaḥ}
"The causes [of this] have been declared: they are the causes for the establishment of particulars through general words. (Vākyapadīya 2.315cd and 316cd)

And thus, even though Tārkṣya was initiated, this question of his is understood as being for the sake of attaining such scriptural knowledge as he did not yet possess through his own discernment of the scriptures, rather than being directed toward one who already possesses that knowledge.
Then, having been addressed in this way, Hara, whose crest-jewel is the shimmering moon, spoke this reply:
Vṛtti: [Commentary]

Thus, having been questioned by Vainateya— who, preceded by praise and an initial inquiry, sought a clarification of the subject matter of the treatise— the venerable Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, his moon-crest quivering with particular intensity due to the shaking of his head born of astonishment, spoke.
Furthermore, what did he say? The Blessed One said:
"What you have asked is excellent; listen to this knowledge of great consequence. (KirT 1.11)
The great tantra named *Kiraṇa* bestows the bliss of supreme nectar; it is all-encompassing, pure, and clearly illuminates the nature of reality. *KirT* 1.12.
Commentary:

Regarding that which you have asked me to state—the auspicious scripture that accomplishes the welfare distinct from the fruits of all other treatises—listen, for it is now being declared; this is the formal promise (*pratijñā*).
For this very reason, since the word *bhadra* itself serves the purpose of auspiciousness and so forth, there is no fault in not employing the word *atha*, even though this is the opening aphorism.

And because its arising is "great"—meaning it is characterized by success that cannot be overcome by the establishment of other philosophical systems—the purpose of this treatise has been stated by this [phrase].
For this very reason, it is called the *Kiraṇa* (The Ray) because it illuminates such a reality;
and it is "great" because it is impelled by the Supreme Lord.
By the word "tantra," its authority is stated;
for the authority of a scripture arises precisely from its being composed by Īśvara,
not from its being uncreated, as that is impossible.

Since the creation does not deviate from its creator, and because it is supreme (*para*) due to pervading all objects and immortal (*amṛta*) as it is imperishable, it is "supreme immortality" (*parāmṛta*). That bliss is supreme perfection, the manifestation of omniscience and agency.
It "gives" that [bliss], meaning it manifests it by way of being a means.
[Quotation: According to the venerable Rāmakaṇṭha in his commentary on the *Kiraṇa*, the great tantra named *Kiraṇa* bestows the bliss of the supreme nectar (*parāmṛta*).
In this context, "supreme" (*para*) refers to that which is all-pervasive; and "immortal" (*amṛta*) refers to that bliss which is indestructible. "Supreme" (*parā*) signifies perfect fullness.
The manifestation of omniscience and omnipotence is manifested by means of that which bestows it; thus, it is said to "bestow the bliss of supreme nectar."
This aforementioned characteristic of liberation is another purpose [of the treatise]. (Jñānaprakāśa’s *Śivajñānabodhavṛtti*, pp. 23–4)
The relationship here, characterized by the nature of means and end and so forth, is established by the context.
However, for all devotees, beginning with the Brahmins, it is the "grasper"— that is, the acceptor— following after the descent of power (*śakti*).

The meaning is that, however, without the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), even one who possesses merely the Brahmin caste does not have the status of being a subject for the most distinguished [initiation].
It is called "pure" (*śubhra*) because it is endowed with the splendor of the four quarters that will be described hereafter.
The phrase "not having a nature that is maimed or shattered by meaninglessness" is a description of its distinguished essential character (*svarūpa*).

By the words "it illuminates the six categories of meaning—the masses of referents (*artharāśi*) such as the 'livestock' and so forth, which are to be discussed hereafter"—its subject matter (*abhidheya*) is stated.
By the word "clearly," its distinction from other compendia (*saṃhitā*) is indicated.
For these [verses] illuminate the meanings of the words by making them non-obscure; therefore, the meaning is that their purpose has not been previously understood.

And thus, the essential nature, the un-understood meaning, the authority, the qualification of the practitioner, the connection, the subject matter, and the purpose of the treatise have been stated. This very first aphorism, "Now, therefore, beginningless, middleless, and endless... and so forth, is of the nature of a formal proposition (*pratijñā*), according to the venerable *Rauravāgama*.
Now, therefore, [is taught] the ladder of bondage for the subtle atom, which is like that which has no beginning, middle, or end. (*Rauravasūtrasaṅgraha* 1:1a)
And because the first aphorism is of such a nature, as in the venerable *Mataṅga* [Tantra]: "Now, the ladder for the bondage of the atom... (*athāṇorbandhasopāna*) and so forth. (*Mat/VP/ 2:1a*)

However, we shall demonstrate that the passage beginning with "not [the relation of] the bound and the bond" (*na tu paśupāśa*) is actually a subsequent sūtra, as it functions as a formal proposition (*pratijñā*) for another meaning indicated by this [preceding] one.

As for the objection raised here—that the mention of the relationship (*sambandha*) and so forth need not be made because they are already established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—and the rebuttal offered by someone that they must nevertheless be stated because they serve as a cause for doubt (*saṃśaya-hetu*) just as in common worldly usage, that is entirely incorrect.
This is because this sūtra, like a worldly sentence and unlike treatises on logic (*tarka-śāstra*), does not establish its point through mere verbal expression alone.

Since this scripture, composed by the Supreme Lord, is an authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), how could its subject matter be doubtful? For a means of knowledge consists in the ascertainment of its own object of cognition, and its fruit is the cessation of doubt regarding that object.
Therefore, it should be countered here precisely by establishing the certainty of the relationship [between words and their meanings] and so forth.
Now, what is its purity?
What kind of categories (padārtha) are those for which this has been stated as an indicator? And how many in number are they? To address these points, there is this other sūtra of formal proposition.
It sets forth the investigation of the knowledge concerning the Lord, the fettered souls, and the fetters;
it is endowed with ritual action and conduct, and brings about the abundance of yogic power.
Commentary: Because the word *paśu* (bound soul) is not applied to those who are stainless, it denotes only those selves who possess impurity (*sāmala*).
And although they are many, they are of two types according to the distinction between the *sakala* (with parts/limitations) and the *akala* (without parts).
In this context, the *sakala* (those with parts) are of two types: those with subtle bodies and those with gross bodies.
The *akala* (partless) are likewise of two types: the *vijñānākala* and the *pralayākala*.
All of these are *paśus* (bound souls), denoted by the word *paśu*; thus, "the bound soul" (*paśu*) is said here to be one category of entity.
The fetters (pāśas),
however, are impurity (mala), karma, and māyā; these belong to those bound souls (paśus).
"Threefold," according to Rāmakaṇṭha (*Īśana*, Vol. III, p. 23):
[these are] the impurity, karma, and māyic [fetters]; they are the threefold [fetters] of those bound souls (*paśu*).
For thus it is: for the *vijñānakevalin*, there is only impurity (*mala*);
for the *pralayakevalin*, there is both impurity and action (*karman*);
but for the *sakala*, there are the bonds (*pāśa*) consisting of impurity, action, and *māyā*.
And for some, [liberation occurs] either through the knowledge, yoga, and renunciation [of the self], or through the exhaustion of karma by means of experience,
solely by the force of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*).
The verse reads "either through enjoyment or through the exhaustion of karma" to provide the final metrical quarter.
Because the body is maintained like the spinning of a wheel, these two [impurities] consist solely of *mala* and *māyā*; we shall explain all of this in detail later.
In this context, *mala* is indeed one, yet it possesses multiple powers that veil many individual souls (*puruṣa*).
It is not a separate ontological principle (*tattva*) from the principle of bondage (*paśutattva*), because without it, the state of being a bound soul would be impossible;
however, it certainly exists as a distinct entity.

Karma also is not a separate reality from the eightfold states such as dharma and so forth, because it consists of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of *prakṛti*; for without that [karma], bondage of *prakṛti* would be impossible.
It is indeed infinite, being diverse due to its manifold nature as various causal conditions (*pratyaya*), and distinct for each individual soul (*puruṣa*) because it must be performed by each one.
However, that which belongs to Māyā—consisting of the thirty principles (*tattva*) beginning with *kalā* and ending with earth—is distinct for each soul in the form of the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*).

Furthermore, we shall explain that [the gross body] is non-different from the three hundred and ninety worlds as their very essence, yet it is both differentiated and non-different in each individual world by virtue of being a gross body composed of the elements; for the gross body is also an object of enjoyment for other selves.
Māyā, too, is a bond (pāśa) because it is the source of bonds.

The power of concealment (*tirobhāvana-śakti*), manifested by the Lord who presides over the womb of *māyā*, is also a bond (*pāśa*); thus, this entire collection of objects is here called the second category, the "bond.

As for the Lord, he is the Blessed One (*bhagavān*) [Śiva], distinguished by the two principles (*tattva*) of Śiva and Sadāśiva, and by the fivefold division of worlds (*bhuvana*), which will be described as consisting of five groups of worlds.

The Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), who will be described [in Kir. 8:139–41], is called the third category along with the liberated souls (muktas). And by the term "knowledge" (jñāna)—understanding it as that by which something is known—the category of Power (śakti) is designated here as the fourth, characterized as the principle of Īśvara and associated with the four worlds (bhuvanas) to be described.
Because knowledge cannot arise for persons without that presiding presence, [it is] "endowed with the four worlds to be described" (Kir. 8.138c–139a).
And likewise, there is also a Vedic revelation: "May he who impels our thoughts [from on high].
(Ṛgveda 3.62.10)
It deliberates upon the creation, dissolution, and so forth of the universe— both its common and specific natures— in accordance with the karma of individual persons; thus,

"deliberation" (*vicāra*) here refers to the category of the fifth principle (*padārtha*), wherein the mass of objects (*artharāśi*) consisting of the two principles of *vidyā* and *vidyeśa*, divided into twenty-six worlds (*bhuvana*), is expounded.
The connection with the promised subject is that one should listen to this scripture, which consists of the *vidyāpāda* and expounds these five categories (*padārtha*).
However, it should not be explained as "listen to this scripture which expounds both the knowledge and the investigation— inference— of the bound soul (*paśu*), the fetters (*pāśa*),
and the Lord (*pati*)," because such an interpretation would lack logical consistency, since a scripture is essentially composed of words.
For knowledge is not derived from the word;
this is because it is designated as the signifier (vācaka) by virtue of its conventional relationship with the signified (vācya).
Rather, it is the object itself;
knowledge, however, is to be inferred from that.

Alternatively, the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) here is used for the sentence which is the cause of the knowledge of the meaning—such as [the knowledge] of cattle and so forth—and the word "investigation" (*vicāra*) is also explained as the logical mark (*liṅga*) which is the cause for inferring that [sentence].

Even so, since there is no distinction between these two [interpretations] regarding their application here— given that both involve abandoning their conventional meanings— it is better to maintain that they refer exclusively to categories of objects (*padārtha*); thus,
the establishment of the five categories of objects is achieved.
As it is stated in the venerable *Raurava*:
"The five categories are renowned as having emerged from the mouths of the Vidyeśvaras."
And briefly:
ritual procedure, action, aspect, yoga, and Śiva—this is the summary. (Rauravaśāsana 4:48); cf. *vidhiḥ kriyā kalā yogaḥ śivaśceti samāsataḥ*.
"In the unsurpassed Śaiva scripture, five categories are to be known:
briefly stated, they are Vidhi, Kriyā, Kalā, Yoga, and Śiva. (Quoted by Alaka on Haravijaya 6:147).
Thus, the previous explanation alone is appropriate:

*kriyā* means ritual action, consecration, or initiation (*dīkṣā*); *caryā* means conduct, the performance of daily rites and so forth. The meaning is: "Listen to this scripture which is endowed with—i.e., possesses as its two constituent parts—the pair of feet consisting of *kriyā* and *caryā*, being equal to and joined with those two."

Yoga is the connection of the mind with the object to be meditated upon; its manifestation is concentration (samādhi) in the form of one-pointedness, which is brought about through the non-deficiency of the limbs such as withdrawal (pratyāhāra). The "burden" (bhāra) of that manifestation is the appearance of infinite fruits.
The treatise which brings this about—listen to it. This is the formal promise (pratijñā) for the fourth quarter (pāda); thus, by implication, the number of quarters is also understood here.

The sixth category of reality (*padārtha*) is said to be the object to be established by the three preceding categories— action (*kriyā*) and so forth— which is described as the category of means (*upāya-padārtha*) in the *Śrīmataṅga* and other scriptures.

Furthermore, the establishment of the true nature of this object is free from defect, because, just as in the case of the Vedic scriptures (*śruti*) and other treatises, there is a single authorial agency across various *saṃhitās*, which resolves the doubts arising from discrepancies between them.
Thus,
this treatise consists of four quarters and expresses six categories;
such is the meaning of this incidental introductory sūtra.
On this point, the prima facie position is as follows; Garuḍa said: "If that is so, then what kind of animal is it that is bound, and how?"
Tell me how one is liberated, so that my doubt may be dispelled.
Commentary: If it is thus that the six categories beginning with the animal have been indicated by you as subjects to be explained,
then one must first state the definition of that animal which has been included as the first category, since:
The followers of the Sugata maintain that this [world] is impermanent because it consists of a stream of consciousness that perishes at every moment;
certain knowers of the Vedānta consider it impermanent because it is an effect of Brahman;
whereas the Naiyāyikas and others hold it to be eternal.
Thus, according to the Cārvākas, [the self] consists of the four great elements;
whereas according to the Vaiśeṣikas and others, it is distinct from them.
Likewise, according to the Sāṃkhyas, even in the state of bondage, its nature is that of a knower and it is a non-agent, just as it is in the state of liberation.
However, according to the Jaiminīyas and others, the self is both a knower and an agent;
according to the Naiyāyikas and others, it is endowed with nine qualities—namely, intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and mental impression;
whereas according to the Sāṃkhyas, it is devoid of qualities.
Thus, according to those who advocate human effort (*puruṣakāra*), the Lord is independent; according to those who advocate destiny (*daiva*), He is not independent;
and likewise, according to the Digambaras and the Vedāntins who maintain the doctrine of the birth of the soul (*jīva*), He is non-pervasive.
Furthermore, because we have encountered various unstable and fallacious arguments—such as those by the Naiyāyikas and others asserting that [the Buddha] is "omnipresent"—we have fallen into doubt.

Therefore, for the sake of dispelling this, you must explain: which of these positions is favored by this omniscient one through his philosophical system such that it is authoritative due to its consistency with scripture, and which is not favored such that it is non-authoritative due to its contradiction with scripture?

Furthermore, as for how it is bound: by what manner? Is it bound solely by the body and the senses, as the Naiyāyikas and others hold, or is it bound also by the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, as the Sāṃkhyas and others hold? This is the doubt.
Moreover, as for how it is liberated: is it liberated by knowledge alone, as the Sāṃkhyas and others hold?
Is it by yoga, as in the case of the followers of Patañjali and others; or by renunciation, as in the case of the Vedāntins; or by ritual action, as in the case of the followers of Jaimini?
As they say:
"One should perform obligatory and occasional rites with the desire to avoid transgression."
Regarding the obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), optional (*kāmya*), and prohibited (*niṣiddha*) [rites], [this is] the refutation of the objection concerning their relationship.
(110) Sloka. {sambandhākṣepaparihāra} (Refutation of the Objection Concerning the Relationship) 110.}
"One seeking liberation should not engage in those [actions] that are either desired or prohibited.
Thus, there is doubt here as well; therefore, it must be explained in order to remove that doubt.
Now follows the established conclusion for the removal of the eightfold doubt.
The Blessed One said:
"The individual soul (paśu) is eternal, indeed formless, ignorant, inactive, devoid of qualities, and powerless;
it is all-pervasive, situated within the belly of Māyā, and intent upon seeking the means for its own enjoyment."

Commentary: By the scriptural statement regarding eternality, there is here a support for the reasons perceived by the Naiyāyikas and others, while setting aside the views of the Buddhists and others.
Furthermore, [it says] "immaterial" (amūrta).

That which possesses form (*mūrti*)—that is, solidity—is "formed" (*mūrta*); such an object, consisting of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), is said not to be of that nature [of consciousness]. Thus, by rejecting the doctrine of the sentience of the elements (*bhūtacaitanyavāda*), there is an endorsement of the reasons observed by the Buddhists and others to establish its distinctness from them. Furthermore, [it is stated] that the ignorant one is inactive in the state of non-manifestation (*akalāvasthā*).
Being devoid of both knowledge and action in every state,

like saltless soup, one who possesses little knowledge and performs little action— this is the acceptance of the position of the Jaiminīyas and others, by way of rejecting the Sāṃkhya and other systems.

By the term "devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇa*), there is an endorsement of the qualitylessness (*nirguṇatva*) seen by the Sāṃkhyas and others, through the rejection of the nine qualities of the self—such as cognition, pleasure, and pain—as perceived by the Naiyāyikas and other schools. By the term "not a lord" (*aprabhu*), limited sovereignty is expressed as before. Now, this [description] favors both those who advocate human effort (*puruṣakāra*) and those who advocate destiny (*daiva*), since each holds one part of the truth: he is a "lord" only with respect to various rites such as the *agniṣṭoma*, which have visible and invisible fruits to be acquired now; however, regarding the enjoyment of karma acquired previously, he is indeed "not a lord."

By the term "pervasive" (*vyāpin*), there is a refutation of those who propound that the *jīva* and *pudgala* are non-pervasive, thereby favoring the Naiyāyikas and others who maintain their pervasiveness.
For this very reason—because [the author] knows all other scriptures and philosophical systems (darśanas)—no logical reasons for establishing the eternity of the self and so forth were stated here.

Even without those [reasons], just as a doubt regarding whether a post or a person might be resolved by the statement of a reliable person (*āpta*) such as "this is a post," or as a doubt regarding a wheel might be resolved by favoring one of its two sides, or by favoring the reasons stated therein; [so too is the case here].
Because their [the reasons'] establishment is already accomplished through cessation, they are useless;

or rather, by this [statement], the self is established as being proven by experience, since there is no need for reasons once something is established by experience— just as in the case of "this jar is red and round," no reason is possible because it is established by experience.

Likewise, since the nature of the grāhaka (the apprehending subject) is established by experience as illuminating both itself and other objects, its stability is likewise established by experience, because it is understood in that way.
Thus, what is the use of a logical reason here?
Nor should it be argued that, in the case of that [subject] being momentary, stability is merely superimposed through delusion—as occurs with time and so forth.

We have demonstrated in the *Mataṅgavṛtti* that because conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are non-conceptual with respect to their own nature due to the contradiction of an action [acting] upon itself, superimposition (*adhyāropa*) is impossible. (Source: *Mataṅgavṛtti*, ad VP 6.24ab)
Therefore, it must be understood from that very source.

Furthermore, it has been demonstrated by us in the *Nareśvaraparīkṣāprakāśa* that momentariness cannot be established here by means of an inference characterized by the impossibility of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) for a stable entity, because that [inference] is also afflicted by defects such as being unestablished (*asiddha*). {As shown by us in the Nareśvaraparīkṣāprakāśa}

Therefore, it should be noted: furthermore, its incorporeality is established by experience alone, as previously stated, through its manifestation as that which perceives [objects] as distinct from the body—which consists of the great elements characterized by form and endowed with touch—by virtue of being the grasper thereof.
There is a negation of [the soul] being composed of the elements (*bhūta*).
For this very reason, because it is experienced as distinct from that which has arisen from the elements, its origination from the elements does not occur.

Furthermore, since it is established as eternal due to its beginninglessness—demonstrated by the observation of purposeful activity preceded by memory, which arises from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of experiences in previous births for every successive birth—this has been shown in the *Rauravavṛttiviveka*.
Thus it has been demonstrated by us in the *Paramokṣanirāsakārikās* within the *Rauravavṛttiviveka*. (Paramokṣa 44–6)
And it has been stated by others:
"The first [stage] is the arrangement of the instruments; [the second is] the upward movement of the vital breath. (Ādyaḥ)
And [it is] prior sensation;
see *Vākya* 1:130, quoted in *Paramokṣa*.
And as it is said [in *Narapati-jayacaryā* 1:19, p.
45]: "The affliction of the bodily locations does not occur without prior experience.
Likewise, his limited knowledge, agency, and slight sovereignty are established by experience, just as before.

In this way, even the qualitylessness (*nirguṇatva*) of cognition, pleasure, pain, and so forth is established, because they are experienced as being occasional—like a jar or other objects—and because they are experienced as having properties contrary to that [qualityless nature] by virtue of being objects of apprehension.

For it has been demonstrated by us in the *Nareśvaraparīkṣāprakāśa* that the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), which is of the nature of the grasper of various objects of apprehension either successively or simultaneously, is indeed always undivided, as is proven by experience.
(Quotation)
Its all-pervasiveness (*vyāpitva*) has also been demonstrated by us in the *Nareśvaraparīkṣāprakāśa* (ad 1.22, pp. 52–6) as its being the grasper [of objects] without limitation by space and time.
Because it manifests in its own immediate form, it is not logical for the subject to be delimited by an object, such as a jar;
as they say:
"That entity whose existence is undelimited by space and time..."
"The existence [of the deity] is not limited [in time]; therefore, it is declared to be eternal.
(Tantravārttika 2.1.5)
"They desire that [Self] to be eternal and all-pervading; thus the pervasiveness of the Self is established.
In order to show that the proof of this [Self], which is endowed with all attributes, is established through direct experience alone, no logical reasons have been stated here.
The Śruti also says thus:
Everything shines only after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined. (Kaṭhopaniṣad 5.15cd)
Thus, there is no contradiction between Śvetāśvataropaniṣad 6:14cd and Muṇḍakopaniṣad 2.2.11cd.

Thus, having first set aside the sixfold doubt concerning the animal—which arises from observing many animals whose natures are mutually contradictory—the variety of locations for this [animal] according to its different states, as established in our own system, is now described:
"It stands within the belly and the end of Māyā. Among these, the *pralayakevalin* (the isolated soul in dissolution) resides within the belly of Māyā.
The distinction is that [the Vijñānakevalin] is at the end of Māyā, specifically upon its summit;
however, if one were to explain "end" as simply the interior of Māyā, the qualification would be entirely fruitless.
For this very reason, the question will concern the Pralayakevalin.
"How is it that he remains within the belly of Māyā? [Kir. 2:6b]
But it is not "within the belly of Māyā.

Rather, since the entire means of experience (*bhogopāya*), consisting of the body and its instruments (*kāryakaraṇa*) and so forth, is situated there as the thinker and the experiencer, he is said to be "located therein" (*tatrastha*).
As he will state: "Thus, bound by the *tattvas* and the *kalās*, he is composed of them (*tanmaya*)."
From Śiva, *kalā* comes into connection with that impure [soul].
Commentary: By the word "of that" (*tasya*), there is a reference specifically to the bound soul (*paśu*) under discussion.

In this context, it should not be explained as referring to one who is "impure" (*aśuddha*) or "possessed of impurity" (*malayukta*); nor does it refer to the "sakala" (the embodied soul) who is "endowed with the *kalās*" and so forth, because that will be described in due order later on. Rather, it refers to one who is "endowed with impurity and karma" (*malakarmayukta*). Therefore, the meaning is this: for that bound soul (*paśu*) who is indeed endowed with impurity and karma, the connection with the *kalās* occurs, but not for the *vijñānakevalin* who is devoid of karma.
As he will say:
"One experiences enjoyment according to one's own karma."
From the very power of employing this qualification, the nature of the *vijñānakevalin* (the soul isolated by knowledge) is determined here.
Furthermore, in the context of *kalā*, "state of being an object of enjoyment" (*bhogyatva*) is said to mean "limitedness" (*parimitatva*).
For this very reason, its status as an effect and its insentience are established, just like those of a jar and other such objects.
He will explain its cause in the fourth chapter. (See *Kiraṇavṛtti* 4.17–22.)
In this context, however, only the state of being a bond with respect to the person (*puruṣa*) is established;
and that [bond] comes into connection with Śiva through him.

For this very reason, it is said to be "due to insentience and lack of autonomy," and this should also be understood to apply to the other principles (*tattva*) that will be described hereafter, because they too are limited.
As he will say:
"Thus bound by the digits of reality (*tattva*)."

The meaning of this [verse] is as follows: whatever is insentient enters into a relationship with something else only when impelled by an agent endowed with specific knowledge and action, like a jar or similar objects.
Since the *kalās* and other categories are insentient, they too are connected with the *puruṣa* only when impelled by an agent endowed with specific knowledge and action.
Furthermore, the determination of the category of the "Lord" (pati) as Śiva—who is that very agent—is established right here;

nor is there any inconclusiveness (anaikāntika) due to [the existence of] air and so forth, because those too have been included within the subject of the argument (pakṣīkṛta). This is shown by the statement beginning with "The effect is gross and manifold," and so on.
However,
since its determination will also arise from the reason of its being an effect (*kāryatva*), there is no contradiction.
[Objection: But surely time itself is unestablished; how then can an agent be established through its impelling? [Reply:
To this it is said:
"One whose consciousness is empowered by that [time], and for whom the object-sphere is manifested by ignorance... (KirT 1.16).
Colored by passion and yet being the primary principle through its nature as the qualities (guṇas),
the bound soul (paśu) is fettered due to its connection with the array of instruments beginning with the intellect (buddhi).
Commentary: That person whose consciousness (*caitanya*) has been empowered—that is, rendered capable—by that *kalā* through the removal of impurity (*mala*), is so described.

This is what is meant: for the person whose existence is established by the reasoning to be explained hereafter, there must necessarily exist, even in the state of being a *sakala* (embodied soul), some limited object that removes the impurity consisting of the veil over perception (*dṛk*) and action (*kriyā*).

Otherwise, for those liberated souls (kevalins) at the time of dissolution, there would be the impossibility of experiencing any object whatsoever through consciousness. That [experiencer] cannot be the *puruṣa*, because as before, it lacks the capacity;
nor can it be *karman*, for the same reason, and because its existence is established by the fact that experience could not otherwise be accounted for.

For a thing whose existence is established through the otherwise inexplicable nature of a particular effect (*kāryāntarānyathānupapatti*), and which is entirely beyond the senses, cannot be determined as the cause of another effect; for that would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of having to postulate other causes such as multiple sense organs. Therefore, neither the sense organs nor the Lord [can be its cause]. That which negates them is *kalā*; thus, by means of the bondage characterized as *kalā*, one is first bound.
Following that, he is so described because his sphere of experience is made known by *vidyā*.

For even in the case of a person whose impurities have ceased, there must necessarily be another instrument (*karaṇa*) for the consciousness consisting of the functions of the intellect (*buddhivṛtti*)—such as memory, intuition, and conceptualization—which will be discussed later; this is because it is a form of consciousness, just like the consciousness of sense-objects through the senses.
And in this case, the intellect (*buddhi*) cannot be the instrument, because it is itself the object [of that consciousness].

Furthermore, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and the rest cannot be considered instruments here either, because they will be described later as performing other functions such as sustaining the body; thus, their status as instruments is not established in this context. Therefore, that which is the instrument there is *vidyā*; this establishes another type of bondage.
Furthermore, one who is colored by passion—which consists of attachment—is bound.

This is the meaning: this passion directed toward objects, which consists of attachment, is not a property of the object itself, because it consists of a vibration within the internal self (adhyātman) and because it would follow that there could be no one free from passion.
Nor is it a property of the intellect (buddhi) characterized by non-detachment.

It cannot be of the nature of an entity, because it would be imperceptible due to its existence in the form of a latent impression (*vāsanā*). Nor can it consist of an active state (*vṛtti*), because even when there is a recollection of something desirable, that [state] is not observed in one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*).
Furthermore, it has been stated that it is not like the removal of impurity in the case of karma and so forth.
By process of elimination, that whose property it is is passion (*rāga*); the other is bondage (*bandha*).
Therefore, *pradhāna* becomes connected with the forms of the qualities such as *sattva*, and with the form of the gross world.

By the use of the word "and" (ca), it is implied that time and the other factors, together with the principles (tattvas) beginning with earth which will be described hereafter, are connected both by way of their own respective qualities and by way of the form of the worlds (bhuvana).
Thus, like the creation of the principles (tattva-sarga), the creation of the worlds (bhuvana-sarga) is also stated here as a form of bondage.
Consequently, there are the instruments (karaṇa) characterized as intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāra), and mind (manas), which are well-known in the Sāṃkhya and other systems.

Furthermore, because of its connection with the five organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*), the five organs of action (*karmendriya*), and that tenfold group of other effects consisting of the primary elements (*bhūta*) and subtle elements (*tanmātra*), it is bound; this supports the theory of bondage of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth as established in the Sāṃkhya and other systems according to the method to be explained hereafter, and not the view of the Vaiśeṣikas and others who hold that the body, senses, and self alone are bound.

For this very reason, in this context, only those bonds such as *kalā* and so forth—which are not established in other philosophical systems—are presented by way of their effects; whereas those bonds well-known in other systems are merely restated because they are already established. Thus, there is no fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*) due to the failure to state their definitions.
For this same reason, even the nature of the bond consisting of necessity (*niyati*) is presented by way of its effect.
Then, "from necessity," and so forth; then, due to the connection with necessity (*niyati*), one is constrained even regarding that which has been acquired by oneself.
*Vṛtti*:

Then, following the connection between the body and the instruments [of action], there occurs a conjunction or relation through *niyati* (destiny); for that reason, the person is constrained by the fruits of karma accumulated previously.

The meaning is this: the restriction of persons regarding the fruits of karma is not caused by the karma itself, because—like the act of plowing and so forth—that karma is useful only for the production of its own specific fruit.

Nor is it caused by another principle (*tattvāntara*), because those [principles] are established by their own effects alone, and there is no evidence for their being the cause of any other effect; as has been stated.

Therefore, just as in agriculture and other such activities there must be someone appointed by the king as a supervisor, so too here there must be a regulator. This regulator is another bond called *niyati* (destiny).

For this very reason, although it will be described later as an effect of *māyā*, its operation occurs only after the connection between the body and the organs has been established; hence its mention is placed later here.

Likewise, there is no fault in the case of time as well. Now, it is asked: in what manner is [the self] regulated by destiny? It is said: "By time, one is deluded regarding the reckoning of time and the experience of its effects. (KirT 1.18)
Commentary:

Time possesses an effect characterized by number, such as "long" or "quick," but direction does not possess [such] effects as *krośa* or *yojana*, nor does number possess [such] effects as "hundred" or "thousand. For that reason, one who is deluded regarding enjoyment by means of time is constrained by necessity (*niyati*).
Because time, too, is a cause for experiencing [the results of karma]; as they say:
"Alas, after a long time you have finally been obtained; I know not what I should do. (cirēṇa bata)
"devdot nigirāmi kim" (Source unknown). It is also quoted with "bhavantīm" for "pibāmi" at the end.
"Shall I enter into the limbs? Shall I drink? Shall I swallow? Thus [it is asked].
And because that [state] is not well-known as a cause of enjoyment, it is presented here by way of its effects.
In its own nature, it is indeed established by the Vaiśeṣikas and others; as they say:
"Time has the cognition of 'long' and 'quick' as its inferential mark.
(kālaścirakṣiprapratyayaliṅgaḥ)
Cf. {Padārthadharmasaṅgraha} p.63,
lines 15–16.} or a paraphrase of {Vaiśeṣikasūtra} 2.2.7.} As for that which is proclaimed by them regarding its eternality and so forth, as they have said:
Those who know time understand it as a substance that is eternal, one, all-pervading, possessed of magnitude, and active.
"Those who know time understand that time exists apart from [any] activity. (Quoted in *Vākya* 3.9.1 and also cited ad *Mata* VP 12:3–4, p. 337.)
Because it will be stated that [the world] is an effect of that māyā.

And as to how differentiation by way of the distinctions of past, future, and present is not accepted here, it has been stated by us in the *Matangavṛtti*; therefore, it should be understood from that very source.
As it is stated in the *Mataṅgavṛtti* (on the twelfth chapter of the *Vākyapadīya*):
"Now, the nature of these principles beginning with *kalā*, their non-pervasiveness, and their being preceded by the gross body are explained."
Thus, bound by the categories of reality (tattva-kalā), possessing limited knowledge and joined with a body,
embraced by the enjoyment of māyā, identified with that, and veiled by the innate (sahaja), [the soul remains in bondage].
Commentary:

These principles, beginning with *kalā* and ending with *kṣiti*, have been previously mentioned; they are called "the *kalās*" because they will be described as effects (*kārya*), and because, while being manifest (*vyakta*), they are non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*).
As it has been stated by the Sāṃkhyas: "Because [the effect] will be described as being an effect" (Kir. 4:22–3).
It (the manifest) has a cause, is non-eternal, non-pervasive, active, manifold, dependent, and indicative;
the unmanifest is the opposite.

"The manifest (vyakta) is composed of parts and is dependent; the unmanifest (avyakta) is the opposite. Thus, bound by those [qualities] in the manner described, the "entire" (sakala) one—meaning one who has not yet obtained an external body or whose external body has perished—exists in the form of a subtle body (sūkṣmadeha).
For if these [elements] were pervasive, the existence of a subtle body would be untenable; as it has been stated:
"The intermediate state body was refuted by Vindhyavāsin.
(antarābhavadehastu niṣiddho vindhyavāsinā)
*Sloka* {Ātmavāda 62ab}:

Being bound by the subtle elements (*tattva-kalā*) and joined with the gross body, one becomes a possessor of limited knowledge (*kiñcijjña*), but not when unbound by them; thus, by demonstrating another distinction of the *sakala* (the conditioned soul), it is stated that even the creation of the elements constitutes a bondage. And the person joined with the gross body—being related to *māyā*, and being "enjoyed" or experienced as *māyā-bhoga*—is embraced and pervaded by that delusion which consists in the conceit of self in what is not-self.
Being absorbed in that, one comes to possess the conceit of a self in what is not-self;
one does not consider the self to be distinct from the body and the instruments [of action].
We shall explain that this very thing constitutes the delusive power of *māyā*.
And it has been stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*: "We shall explain [this]... (*KirV* ad 2:15).
Thus, the atom (aṇu), situated within the collyrium of māyā and obscured by its own defects, is colored [by them].
"Being colored by those enjoyments of *māyā*, he himself attains identity with them. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, the binding nature of impurity (*mala*) consists solely in its quality of being an obscuration, just as a cataract or similar film obscures the eye; this is established in states such as that of the *pralayakevalin* (the isolated soul in dissolution), as expressed in the phrase "covered by innate impurity."
Now, regarding the bondage of karma:
thereafter, due to its own karma, it experiences the entirety of experience, such as pleasure and so forth.
(Vṛtti)

Then, immediately following the connection with the gross body, one experiences results such as pleasure and pain through the medium of mental states (*bhāva*) produced by previously accumulated auspicious and inauspicious karma; thus, it is stated that the creation of mental states (*bhāvasṛṣṭi*) consists of the bondage of karma.

Likewise, even when all karma has been exhausted without remainder, because the body is maintained like the whirling of a potter's wheel due to the persistence of its residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), one experiences enjoyment consisting merely of the perception thereof. By this much, the "other state" of the *sakala* [individual] is bound.
All this regarding the category of *pāśa* (bondage) has been explained in order to resolve the question of how this occurs.
Now, the resolution of the question "How is one liberated? is stated:
When equal karma has arisen, then, by the power of the lapse of time... (KirT 1.20)
When one is initiated by a Guru through the descent of intense power,
he becomes omniscient like Śiva himself, entirely devoid of limited knowledge.
At that time, the transmigrating soul is no longer merely a wanderer, but is fully perfected in the manifestation of its Śiva-nature.
Commentary:
*Kāla* is so called because it "measures" (*kālayati*), i.e., it leads one toward blackness and causes defilement; thus, *kāla* refers to impurity (*mala*).
Because words such as *kāla* (black) and *nīla* (blue) denote specific colors; as they say:
"That which is nothing at all attains another state through its association with the Great Self.
(yanna kiñcidapi...)

Its "interval" (*antara*) is its transformation (*pariṇāma*); its "power" (*vaśa*) is its capacity (*sāmarthya*).
