Since she is established as the illuminator by way of her effect, it is therefore understood that she does not abide as the deluder of the person; this is stated because her existence [as a deluder] is negated by the non-perception of an effect that is contrary to her essential nature.

Furthermore, whatever effect is contradictory to another effect is produced by a cause distinct from the cause of that [first] effect; for example, an effect consisting of darkness, which is contradictory to the effect characterized as light, is produced by a cause distinct from the cause of light.

And since the effect consisting of delusion (*moha*) regarding the person (*pums*) is contradictory to the effect of the person's illumination, it too must be produced by a cause distinct from the cause of the person's illumination.

That cause—which is established here by the inference from the specific nature of the effect—is *mala* (impurity) distinct from *māyā*. This is the intended meaning of this concluding statement, and thus there is no redundancy.
For this very reason, he will conclude: "That [self] is distinct [from the body] by virtue of reasoning. (Kir. 2.17d)

Nor is there any inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatā) here on account of sattva, rajas, and tamas, which are the effects of the unmanifest (avyakta), because they are established as being non-contradictory [to the probandum].
As it has been stated by the Sāṅkhyas:
"The qualities (guṇas) function through mutual suppression, support, production, and companionship."
"The *guṇas* function through mutual suppression, support, generation, and companionship" (Sāṃkhya-kārikā 12cd).
This is also cited in the commentary on *Narasiṃhapurāṇa* 2:15:
"But surely, the Sāṃkhyas maintain that delusion (*moha*) is simply a particular form of illumination, consisting in the conceit of a self in what is not-self."
As it has been said:
"The division of *tamas* is eightfold, that of *moha* is likewise, and *mahāmoha* is tenfold."
"Thus there is *tāmisra*,
and likewise *andhatāmisra* is eighteenfold. (Sāṃkhyakārikā 48)
Therefore, since a contradiction of essential nature (*svabhāvavirodha*) is not established here, how can there be a proof of a distinct impurity (*mala*)?
That is incorrect;
for "manifestation" is expressed by the word *prakāśa*, while "obscuration" is expressed by the word *mala*. (KirT 2.14)
Commentary: This is the meaning—here, this "delusion" (moha) is not intended in its ordinary sense, since the existence of the body itself is already established.

Rather, in order to avoid the consequence of [the Self] being omniscient—which would follow from its nature as consciousness and its all-pervasiveness as will be stated later—one must necessarily accept another kind of delusion, distinct from that, which is denoted by the word "impurity" (mala) and consists of concealment (āvṛti).

And since that [impurity] consists of an obscuration of light, it is in contradiction with the manifestation of the *puruṣa*, which is denoted by the term "manifestation"; thus, there is no lack of proof here regarding the contradiction with the nature of the impurity established as being distinct. Let it be granted that this impurity, being of the nature of an obscuration, causes delusion because it is the cause of ignorance (*ajñāna*); however, as for this so-called "natural" (*prākṛta*) delusion that was mentioned, its nature is that of the manifestation of the *puruṣa*, and therefore that [claim of its being the cause of delusion] is indeed untenable. This is not so, because:
"The impurity is clearly said to be the manifestation of the *guṇas*, like a lamp and darkness."
Commentary:

Just as a lamp, though it is an illuminator, is called "darkness" or "delusion" because it illuminates things such as blue lotuses in a manner contrary to [their true nature], such as by making them appear as red lotuses; so too, the manifestation of the self is [called delusion] because it manifests what is impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self as being permanent, pure, pleasurable, and the self.
Having made [the object] clearly manifest, impurity (*mala*) is declared to be delusion (*moha*).
[This occurs] regarding what is impermanent, impure, suffering, and non-self.
(Cf. *Sarvajñānottaravṛtti*, IFP T.85, p. 6, lines 5–6)
As they say: "Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the perception of the permanent, the pure, the pleasant, and the self in what is impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self.
(See also *Yogasūtra* 2.5).
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the perception of the permanent, the pure, the pleasant, and the self in what is impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self.
This is what is meant:
it is not merely a lack of knowledge, but even erroneous knowledge is indeed delusion (*moha*); thus there is no fault. For this very reason...
Even illusion is said to be deluding through the enjoyment of the savoring of sense objects.
Vṛtti:
By that very form, we [describe him] as "enveloped by the expansion of māyā."
By the passage beginning with *Kir* 1:19c, *māyā* is also said to be delusive;
the meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that it is not only *mala*.
And that [mala] is delusive by means of its effect—the enjoyment (*bhoga*), which is the manifestation (*prakāśa*) consisting of the "taste" (*rasa*) or relish of both the subject and the object;

therefore, we have no dispute here with the Sāṅkhyas. However, the point of contention is precisely that the *mala* has been established as distinct from the natural delusion (*prākṛta-moha*). And thus:
Wherever he may abide, due to the impurity of his own karma, bondage arising from illusion proceeds for him along with its causal conditions.
If [Māyā were distinct], why would even Śiva, who is free from beginningless impurity, not possess it? Therefore, by logical reasoning, Māyā is certainly not distinct from Mala.
Commentary: Just as karma is the instrumental cause for the activity of *māyā* in the person (*pums*) throughout all the worlds from *kalā* down to the earth (*kṣiti*), so too is *mala*.

Otherwise, since it will be stated that [the soul] possesses the nature of consciousness, there would follow the consequence of its being Śiva by virtue of being omniscient and omnipotent; consequently, the very activity of the bondage of *māyā* would not occur.
Now, one might object: "Let karma be the cause for its [the world's] activity; what is the use of impurity (mala)?
It is not so, because for one who is free from impurity, there is no agent—since all such a person is Śiva—and thus those karmas themselves are not established.
The Jainas (Kṣapaṇakas) argue: "Let karma itself be postulated as the obscuration; what is the use of [postulating] a 'mala'?
This is incorrect, because karma is established—as in the case of agriculture and so forth—merely as the cause of its own fruit, and its nature as an obscuration is not observed.

It has been stated that even in the case of the perception of objects and so forth, this same [principle] applies, as it would follow that the sense organs and other factors would be non-existent if one were to postulate that very [mala] as their cause.
Therefore, since activity proceeds from *māyā*, one must admit that *mala* is indeed distinct from *karman*.
For this reason, *māyā* is not *mala*.
And just as that [impurity] is distinct from those [categories], so too has it been established by means of inference based on reasoning; this is the conclusion.
Here, the doubt of the opponent is raised: "All this may be the effect of *māyā*; whence could there be another, innate impurity (*sahaja-mala*)?"
Commentary:
All that is an effect of *māyā*, beginning with *kalā*, would thus constitute a complete bondage consisting of the *tattvas* themselves;
or else, it would consist of all the elements (*bhūta*) and worlds (*bhuvana*) without exception.
This is the meaning: whatever constitutes bondage is that very same reality (tattva) situated within the path (adhvan) as the worlds (bhuvana) and so forth;

just as the effect of Māyā is a bondage, so too has impurity (mala) been described by you as a bondage—it, too, is either a distinct reality or another world within the path, and thus there is both an excess of realities and an excess of worlds.
It would follow [as an absurdity].
Now, if its nature as consisting of reality, the worlds, and so forth is not accepted, then it has been stated that its status as a bond is also unestablished, just like that of a rabbit's horn.
Whence, then, could there be another innate impurity (*mala*)?
To this, the rebuttal is:
"That state of being a bound soul (paśutva) resides within the Self; even the bound soul is situated in the midst of the path. (KirT 2.18)
"By whomsoever [a definition] has been stated, by him that [definition] is considered to be a defect (mala), because its characteristic is different from that [of the cause].

Commentary: This is the meaning—the reason "because of action" (karman) is inconclusive (anaikāntika); for even though it is a bondage, it does not exist in the persistence of the principles (tattva), worlds (bhuvana), and so forth.
Now, it might be argued that because he resides within the *māyātattva*, his object [of experience] is not subject to uncertainty (*anaikāntika*).

To this it is replied: if that were so, then that too would be "cattlehood" (*paśutva*), which is impurity (*mala*) residing in the principle of cattlehood (*paśutattva*); for without that [impurity], the state of being a bound soul (*paśu*) is impossible for individual selves.

Since it exists on the path by means of that [principle], although impurity has a characteristic distinct from the principles and worlds which are the effects of *māyā*, there is no fault in its being a bond like *karman*.
But that which is innate impurity (*sahaja-mala*)—by means of word-breaks such as "māye" and so forth—it is [defined] by force [of the text]:
"The innate impurity is *māyā*. (*sahajaḥ syān malo māyā*, Kir. 2.12a).

He explains the sūtras by turning them toward the side of *māyā* as impurity (*mala*). One who is uncertain regarding the meaning of the scripture must be asked for the reason why *māyā* is considered impurity.

For otherwise, it would not be possible to determine the non-difference of a thing that is entirely beyond the senses and whose difference is established through its effects—just as in the case of the sense organs and so forth—because that would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of there being no difference between the sense organs and the rest, including the *kalās*, and the subtle elements (*tanmātras*).
But was it not stated that the reason [for the non-existence of impurities] is the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of impurities distinct from illusion?
No, because this [reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since it is the presence of something that does not have the nature of a pervader (*avyāpakarūpa*).

For it is only when a pervader is absent that the pervaded is necessarily excluded—just as the absence of a tree excludes a *śiṃśapā* tree—but not in the case of other things such as jars and so forth, as that would lead to the undesirable consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not pervade the existence of the object of cognition (*prameya*), because otherwise it would follow that everyone is omniscient; thus, even when the means of valid cognition has ceased to function, the non-existence of the object is not established. Therefore, in this case regarding the existence of something distinct, doubt alone is appropriate.

Furthermore, this reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), because a means of valid cognition characterized by the perception of an effect incompatible with the nature [of the probandum] regarding the existence of a distinct impurity was stated previously.
As for the objection that there is a contradiction in coexistence because these two effects—consisting of the states of being a *śiva* and a *paśu*—cannot both reside in a single self:

To say that "it does not exist" is also incorrect; for even though these two are not in a state of mutual exclusion (parasparaparihāra-virodha), they consist of mutual non-existence (itaretarābhāva) like a tree and its absence, and thus it is impossible for them to arise from a single cause.
This is precisely the point we have asserted here.
This demonstration of the non-coexistence of these two, even though they are contradictory, is merely the pointing out of a fault, because it does not subvert the intended meaning of the proposition.
Nor is it logical to claim that the state of being a bound soul (paśutva) persists in the self just as the state of Śiva does;
for the former exists as something distinct from the latter, consisting in the form of impurity (mala) which takes on the aspect of a different entity.
And he will say: "Because of its beginningless connection with the self, it is metaphorically designated as *dharma*. (Kir. 2.23cd)

Nor can there be a coexistence of its two effects—illumination and obscuration—due to the distinct states of the self, just as there are distinct states such as "possessing all" (*sakala*) and "not possessing all" (*akala*).

Furthermore, the argument that this reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because the eye and other organs produce contradictory effects such as illumination and non-illumination depending on the presence or absence of auxiliary factors like light is utterly untenable.

For when an auxiliary factor is absent, the organ is observed not to produce its own effect, but it does not produce something contradictory to it; since non-existence (*abhāva*) is not a real entity, it is impossible for it to be produced.

The sun produces light for those such as humans, but not for those such as owls; yet, because that light is extremely brilliant and thus causes injury to their eyes, it is figuratively described as "not illuminating" for them—just as it is for one with weak vision—not because it fails to produce light like darkness.

Consequently, since we perceive an effect contrary to the nature of the previously mentioned [sun] which is free from all defects, it is established that *mala* is indeed distinct from *māyā*. Enough, then, of disputing with those who have cast aside the meaning of the scriptures.
Thus, since the impurity (mala) has been established as distinct from Māyā by means of valid cognition, other synonyms are stated in order to demonstrate its designations according to other Saṃhitās:
"Impurity is ignorance (ajñāna), the state of being a bound soul (paśutva), that which causes obscuration, and darkness (tamas). (KirT 2.19)
For ignorance (avidyā), obscuration (āvṛti), and stupor (mūrchā) are declared to be its synonyms;
and it is established as such through various distinctions of synonyms like "ignorance" and so forth in each respective philosophical system. (KirT 2.20)
Commentary:
Now, is this impurity well-known in other philosophical systems as it is in other scriptural collections?
No, it is said in reply.
"Because of its existence, the bound soul (paśu) is here considered to be one who is to be bound, purified, and awakened.
*Vṛtti*:

Because of the existence of this impurity (*mala*), "here"—that is, in this very system of the Supreme Lord—the bound soul is intended to be one who is to be impelled, bound by means of *kalā* and the other [categories], purified by initiation (*dīkṣā*), and awakened by knowledge consisting of the scriptures.
It is not so in other philosophical systems.
Consequently, it is implied that those described in other systems are merely bound souls (*paśu*), because [in their view] the impurity (*mala*) cannot be severed since it remains unknown to them.
If this is the case, then even the various states of the self, such as being bound (*pāśya*) and so forth, must likewise be beginningless.

Consequently, it would follow that even those [states] are distinct bondages; however, that is incorrect, because it has been proclaimed that the various functions such as *pāśyā* and so forth are merely its own modifications (*bheda*).
When the *sattva* is present, these [functions] come into being, as does the state of being an enjoyer; not merely that alone.
Commentary:

Since the cessation of these functions—such as the power of binding (*pāśyā*) and so forth—is established upon the removal of impurity (*mala*), it is proven that they have impurity as their cause, just as light has a lamp as its cause.
"It is not a separate entity of bondage.

Thus, having refuted by this much that impurity (*mala*) is a non-entity and that its nature is *māyā*, [the author now considers] whether it might instead be a quality (*guṇa*) of the self (*ātman*).
Thus, by restating the third question mentioned previously, the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is presented.
Garuḍa said:
If it is thus established, then this impurity (mala), which is the object of bondage, is associated with the bound soul (paśu).
Why is this impurity not logically postulated as belonging to the self?
*Vṛtti*:

If it is thus established that the self, whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), is the one bound by fetters, then an obscuring impurity must also be postulated for it, because limited knowledge would otherwise be inexplicable.
Well then, let this impurity, which consists of ignorance, be logically postulated through inference as an inherent attribute of the self itself.

As the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas say: "Whatever is produced in a certain locus by some other cause does not exist there [prior to that production], such as light produced by a lamp and the like in the case of darkness;
and consciousness is indeed produced in the self by the body, the sense organs, and so forth."
Therefore, since even that [impurity] does not exist there, it is established that the self is of an ignorant nature; how, then, could there be the establishment of a separate impurity?
To this, the Blessed One spoke the established conclusion:
Because of its beginningless connection with the self, it is metaphorically designated as "dharma."
"How is it that, by being endowed with that knowledge, he has come to possess the quality of ignorance?
[The *Vṛtti* states: "This would indeed be so, if this reason were established for us."
But [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*), because we accept that the body, the sense organs, and so forth function there as manifestors of cognition.
[Objection: Surely the fact that the body, the sense organs, and so forth are the causes of cognition is established by the observation and non-observation of their presence and absence.

[Reply: No, because since those two [presence and absence] can also occur through [their acting as] manifestors, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Thus, the soul's state of being non-cognizant is not established by this unestablished reason.
Therefore, it must necessarily follow that for this impure self, there exists a distinct obscuration (āvaraṇa) with which it has been connected since beginningless time.

Consequently, it should be understood from the scripture that the self is described as "impure" only by way of metaphorical designation due to its association with that [obscuration], and not because its very nature is ignorance.

If that is so, then doubt regarding its state of ignorance in that regard would be appropriate, rather than a certainty of its knowledge; for it is by means of such [certainty] that the existence of a distinct impurity is established.
To this it is replied:
for that [entity], its property would not manifest as a transformation within the state of being a property. (KirT 2.24)

Commentary: Ignorance as an impurity cannot be either a quality (*dharma*) or the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of that self, because it would follow that the self is non-self, like a jar or other such objects.
Alternatively, [the opponent might argue]: "The self is that wherein knowledge arises as inhering."
That too is incorrect.
If that [self] were previously the substratum (dharmin) with respect to ignorance, then even later, its inherence in knowledge would be impossible, just as in the case of a jar or similar objects.

Alternatively, if knowledge is admitted for that which is essentially ignorant, there would clearly be a transformation into another state (rūpāntara-pariṇāma), just like the production of yellowness in an *āmalaka* fruit; this is the fault that will be stated later.

Now, [it may be argued]: "Knowledge is indeed a quality, because, while being perceptible to persons such as ourselves, it is not a visual perception, just like taste and other [qualities]. (See *Kiraṇāvalī* 2.26ab for the fault that will be stated.)

Furthermore, since a quality must necessarily reside in a substance, that which is its substratum—the self—is established as being of the nature of consciousness alone, because it is distinct from those [qualities].
This too is incorrect, because [it is said]:
"In the person, who possesses the attribute of consciousness," and so forth.
If the quality of consciousness were not the inherent nature of the person, he would be subject to transformation.
(Vṛtti:
Consciousness is the very quality—the essential nature—of that which possesses it.
Being thus constituted,
he experiences everything as "I am," and therefore he is the Person (puruṣa).
The self is established for every person through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) by virtue of its being the illuminator of both itself and others; what need is there for any other proof?
[Objection: But has not the reason already been stated—that cognition is a quality (*guṇa*), just like taste and so forth?
[Reply: That too is incorrect, because for us, the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is unestablished in the case of the example.

For entities such as tastes and so forth, being produced only in a state of aggregation and ceasing only in a state of aggregation, are described by us—just like by the Sāṃkhyas, Buddhists, and others—as performing purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), because this is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
However, there is no other substratum for them whatsoever, since nothing distinct from them is perceived.
If that is so, how then is the conventional usage "there is fragrance in the earth" and so forth explained?
It is indeed erroneous, rooted in the habit of false views;
or rather, it is for the purpose of expressing a single part of a distinguished collection, as in the phrase: "The *dhava* tree of the forest is beautiful.
(vanasya dhavaḥ śobhanaḥ)
As stated [in the *Nyāyaratnaprabhā* on *Nyāyasūtra* 1.1.4, p. 11], this is indeed correct.
Therefore, since knowledge itself is not established as a quality (*guṇa*), it has been stated that the self is established as having that very nature [of being the substrate].
If it is argued that because cognition is experienced as impermanent, it must therefore be impermanent, that is incorrect;
for cognition is of two kinds: that which consists of determinate judgment (*adhyavasāya*) and its other [indeterminate] form.

In this regard, that which consists of determinative ascertainment (*adhyavasāya*) is indeed accepted by us as impermanent, since it is a property of the intellect (*buddhi*). However, that knowledge which consists of pure human experience (*pauruṣa-saṃvedana*), being non-determinative in nature, is never perceived as being absent; for it is always experienced in a single form as the subject (*grāhaka*).

Furthermore, there is no impossibility of its performing causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in succession, and all such points have been demonstrated by us at length in the *Nareśvaraparīkṣāprakāśa*; therefore, they should be understood from that very source.
As we have demonstrated in the *Nareśvaraparīkṣāprakāśa* (ad 1.22, p.

52), it is not logical for ignorance (*ajñāna*) to be the nature of impurity (*mala*) in that person (*pums*), whose essence is consciousness (*cit-svabhāva*) because he consists of knowledge (*jñānātmaka*).
Because it would follow that there is a transformation into another form, as in the case of the *āmalaka* fruit and others;
for in one [instance] cognition is manifested, while in another it remains concealed. (KirT 2.25)

Commentary: Since you maintain that cognition arises with respect to one object such as color (rūpa), but when it has arisen with respect to another such as taste (rasa), it is destroyed, it follows that there is a transformation into another form for this self (ātman).
To the question "What is the fault in this?", it is replied:
The transformation of that which is non-conscious [into something conscious] is not tenable.
*Vṛtti*:

That which undergoes transformation is established as non-conscious, just like external objects such as the *āmalaka* fruit; therefore, by virtue of its being subject to transformation, it would follow that the self (*ātman*) is also non-conscious. Thus, in order to avoid this undesirable consequence, the self must certainly not have ignorance (*ajñāna*) as its intrinsic nature.
Rather, it is of the very nature of consciousness itself;
thus, a defilement (mala) that has a distinct nature as its obscurer is established.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of [the mind] being omniscient. In this way, the third question is also refuted.
"If that is so, then this same fault applies even to the position that impurity is distinct [from the self]; thus the challenger objects by way of a cumulative argument.
Garuḍa said:
"Because of their beginningless connection, there can be no separation between the two, despite their omnipresence. (KirT 2.26)
When the destruction of the innate [impurity] occurs, would there not be the destruction of that [soul] as well?
Commentary:

The relationship between those two—the self and the impurity—which is characterized as that of the beginningless veiled and the veiler, is indeed a specific nature (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*). Therefore, there can be no separation or cessation [of that relationship], precisely because it is beginningless, just like the nature of the conscious from the unconscious; thus, there would be no liberation.
Now, if it is maintained that there is a dissociation from that [nature],

then, when the innate nature has been destroyed, its destruction would take the form of the arising of another nature, which is a transformation (pariṇāma); thus, the very same fault remains as was previously stated regarding the position that the impurity is non-different [from the nature].

Now, if it is argued that there is no separation between the two by their own nature, but rather [no separation] due to their mutual conjunction—just as in the case of the eye and its veil—and therefore this fault does not apply, that too is not tenable.
This is because of "pervasiveness," meaning due to being all-pervading;
for separation occurs when that which is non-pervasive is moved to another location from that which is non-pervasive.
Since that which is all-pervading exists everywhere, it is impossible for it to be separated from anything; thus, there would be no liberation.

If, on the other hand, separation is admitted even for such a [pervasive] entity, then, upon the destruction of the innate, coexistent obscuring factor, there must also be the destruction of its nature as the object to be obscured, or else a transformation into another form; in either case, that very same fault remains.
On this point, the Blessed One stated the established conclusion:
"The destruction of even this pervasive impurity and its power is brought about by that [knowledge]. (KirT 2.27)
By means of skillful methods, the power residing in impurity is somehow restrained;
just as the burning power of fire is quickly suppressed by a mantra. (KirT 2.28)
In the same way, due to the obstruction of that power, it is said to be "separated.
[Vṛtti]:
In this regard, first of all, this is not a fault concerning the subject of impurity (*mala*).

For it is indeed the case that not only for this non-pervasive, delusive, and natural impurity (*prākṛtamala*), but even for the pervasive atomic impurity (*āṇavamala*), the destruction—that is, the transformation—of its nature as an obscuring power is effected by means of initiation through mantra, just as the burning capacity of fire is [neutralized].

This occurs "in some way" (*kathañcit*) by interrupting the experience of karma whose effects have already begun, but not entirely; whereas by means of initiation leading to immediate liberation (*sadyonirvāṇadīkṣā*), it is brought about "in its entirety" (*sarvātmanā*) without such interruption.

Furthermore, since it is accepted that impurity (*mala*) is subject to transformation while being eternal, the objection that this would entail the proof of a change into a different nature is not tenable; as it has been stated, this would merely be proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

For this very reason, although the power of impurity remains in its own essential existence through the transformation into a different state of nature, the person is said to be "separated" from it—just as one is said to be separated from a disease—even though there is no actual disjunction of the substance itself.
Therefore, the claim that "this separation does not occur because of omnipresence" is also free from fault.
Now, the defect pertaining to the person (*puruṣa*) is also refuted:
"Having brought about the obstruction of its power, one becomes free from desire for existence. (KirT 2.29)
Commentary: *Śaktisaṃrodha* means the obstruction of power.
Having effected that [obstruction] of that impurity (*mala*), the Supreme Lord makes the person free from desire for existence, devoid of anger, passion, and so forth.

For this very reason, it has been stated that the gurus examine the student for the sake of determining the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) and for the purpose of conferring initiation (*dīkṣā*), by means of signs such as the absence of anger, passion, and so forth.
Consequently, at that time, there is merely a transformation of the impurity (*mala*) into another form, but not a transformation of the self’s own nature into another state.
Therefore, it is stated that the previously mentioned fault does not apply.
For that very nature of [the cognition] which, when impurity (*mala*) exists, apprehends an object independently of that impurity, remains the same even when impurity is absent.
How then, while impurity exists, does it not apprehend the object?
This is the talk of a child.
For how could that which perceives an object independently of impurities exist in their presence?
But surely its object is manifest now, whereas it was not before; so how is there not a transformation into another nature?
That too is incorrect;
for objects, illumination is simply the act of making them its own object, and nothing else.
However, it has been stated that this does not exist within itself at all times independently of impurities.

Therefore, the method of attributing contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*), which would entail the existence of distinct intrinsic natures (*svabhāvāntara*), has been refuted at length in the *Nareśvaraparīkṣāprakāśa*—starting with the argument that [the two] do not have different intrinsic natures as their objects of cognition (*na svabhāvabhedālambanagatatvāt*). [Note:
It is uncertain which specific passage this refers to.]
Therefore, this very point must be understood.

Furthermore, as for the objection raised regarding the defect of a transformation into a different nature—characterized by the removal of the soul's state of being obscured due to the removal of the obscuration that co-exists with it—that too is addressed here: "The innate [impurity] is simultaneous with the copper; yet, upon its destruction, there is no destruction of that [copper]."
Just as there is the depletion of copper [dross], so too is there the depletion of the impurities of the person.

Just as when the husk of rice is removed, there is no destruction of that [grain], so too, by the removal of impurity, no modification occurs to the Self; it is in this respect alone that it serves as an illustration, and not otherwise, for the copper [is subject to change]. Vṛtti: Just as no modification whatsoever is seen in the copper through the removal of the *sahacara* (concomitant) impurities, so also there is no modification of the Self through the removal of impurity; it is by this much that it constitutes an analogy, and not otherwise, as in the case of copper.

This is what is meant: this distinction, caused by the presence or absence of impurity (*mala*), is adventitious (*aupādhika*). It is not the case that the Self—which, independent of impurity, has the singular nature of apprehending objects—possesses another, unobstructed nature that would effect such a distinction. Since there is no transformation into a different intrinsic nature (*svabhāvāntara-pariṇāma*), the previously mentioned fault does not follow. This very position, being established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa-siddha*), is further reinforced by another example established through inference (*anumāna*).
Just as the potency inherent in poison is neutralized by mantras.
In that way, the poison is not destroyed; likewise is the destruction of the impurity of the person (*pums*).
Commentary:

Because it is the cause of delusion and death, even when the innate power (*sahajā śakti*), which stands in the place of the [poisonous] substance, has ceased for the person who stands in the place of the [poison], there is never any destruction of the essential nature of color, form, and so forth; just as in that case, so too for the person.
Regarding the phrase "the destruction of impurity":
since it has been shown partially by way of an illustration, the conclusion of this section is now drawn through another illustration established by direct perception:
"The fruit of the *kataka* tree, when cast into turbid water... (Kir 2.32).
Just as one might obstruct the flow of water by diverting it elsewhere,
so too does the knowledge of Śiva effect the obstruction of [worldly] power for that person.
Commentary:
For example, the fruit of a specific tree called *kataka* is naturally possessed of impurities such as *meghaja* and the like.
The meaning is as follows: it is observed that when a stone is thrown into water, it effects the obstruction of that power characterized by turbidity;
however, it does not cast anything other than its own nature from the water elsewhere. Thus, it merely removes the turbidity itself and nothing else.

Likewise, Śiva alone is "knowledge" (*jñāna*), because he is the cause of knowledge for all by virtue of manifesting the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*). It is said that [this knowledge] is the "obstructor of the power" (*śaktisaṃrodhakāraka*) of that impurity (*mala*), either through initiation (*dīkṣā*) for the sake of producing eligibility for it, or through the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). Alternatively, it refers to the knowledge related to Śiva as the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) which belongs to those initiated; this is the knowledge to be described as a daily obligation (*nityakartavyatā*). Because of initiation, the impurity—which has not yet been exhausted due to the obstruction of the experience (*bhoga*) of karma whose effects have already begun—is diminished every day in its entirety. Thus, [that knowledge] gradually becomes the obstructor of the power of impurity.
But this is not the case for the *puruṣa*.

Consequently, since there is no transformation into another nature even in its constituent part (*aṃśa*), the previously mentioned objection regarding insentience does not apply to the *mala*; rather, it is actually an ornament to it. Thus, there is no fault whatsoever in the position that the *mala* is distinct [from the *puruṣa*].
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Śrīmatkiraṇavṛtti* composed by Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha, son of Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha.
Now follows another chapter, preceded by questions, for the purpose of examining the categories (*padārthas*) themselves.
Here, the relationships between the aphorisms (*sūtra*), the categories, the chapters (*prakaraṇa*), and their connections should be understood as before.
But Pāṭalika, following the establishment of impurity (*mala*) as distinct [from the self], examines whether that very impurity is indeed passion (*rāga*);
thus, although it consists of a statement, it is "colored by passion" (*rāgeṇa rañjitaḥ*).
And thus is the question:
Garuḍa said, "It is taught that the state of being an enjoyer arises from impurity; could it not also arise from desire?"
And since that [affliction] arises from passion and so forth, passion itself must be stated here; what is the use of mentioning "impurity" (mala)?
Vṛtti:
Now, [it may be asked] by the statement beginning with "and obscuration by the word *mala*," etc.
{malaśabdena cāvṛtiḥ}
In *Kir* 2:14d, it is stated that the primary obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) consisting of impurity (*mala*) has the individual soul (*puruṣa*) as its object;
however, the capacity for being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) and so forth are incidental. As it has been said:
The modes of activity such as *pāśyā* and others are proclaimed to be its various divisions;
and not only is there the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*).
"When there is a male, these [qualities] come to be, and not merely the state of being an enjoyer.
What kind of question is this?
Now, the question is: is it not the case that here "being an enjoyer" (bhoktṛtva) is said to mean simply "being unobstructed," and not "having enjoyment as one's sole essence"?

If this is so, then only *mala* (impurity) should be mentioned; what is the use of *rāga* (attachment)? Thus, the question regarding the implication of *rāga* is appropriate, but not the question "what is the use of *mala*?"
"Even in the absence of passion and the like, its effect exists in states such as that of the *pralayakevalin*";

this is true. However, what is being proposed here as the opponent's position is not the absolute absence of impurity (*mala*), but rather the question: "What is the use of impurity regarding the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*)?"

For the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*)—which consists essentially in a single-minded relish for enjoyment—is established by the very attachment (*abhiṣvaṅga*) previously mentioned as the effect of passion (*rāga*); what, then, is the use of postulating *mala* (impurity) here as a cause?
The meaning of the question is that passion alone is the cause here, whether directly or through a succession of causes;
thus, there is no contradiction.

Therefore, the Blessed One spoke of the resolution regarding this very point by accepting the existence of impurity: "That which is called the state of being an enjoyer has as its cause beginningless impurity."
Commentary: This state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) which was previously mentioned by us is beginningless; for it has been stated that impurity (*mala*) is its cause. Therefore...
Because impurity (*mala*) is beginningless, that [state] is also beginningless.

This is what is meant: this state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*), characterized by the capacity for enjoyment, is entirely different from that state of being an enjoyer produced by delusion (*moha*).
It exists in the *pralayākala*, but not in the *vijñānākala*, because of the absence of karma (*karman*).
Just as karma is a cause [for the bound soul], so too is impurity (mala); however, that [impurity] is not possible for the *pralayākala*, who is subject to the grace of the Supreme Lord.
Therefore, it is said that desire (*abhilāṣa*) is not its instrumental cause; for if the body exists, by what cause could that desire arise? (KirT 3.2)
Passion also proceeds because it has that as its cause;
the commentary states:
"This longing also occurs only when this gross body exists."
That body [is so called] because of its connection with attachment and other factors that constitute the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*).
Since the agency of experiencing belongs to those very factors—attachment and the rest—in their active manifestation, how can it be suspected that desire is the cause of this [agency]?
For even this attachment and the rest, which are the causes of desire, have that [subtle body] as their cause.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"Just as a man's imprisonment in fetters depends upon the seed of his theft. (KirT 3.3)
In this way, the principle of attachment (*rāgatattva*) proceeds by depending upon the state of being a bound soul (*paśutva*).

Commentary: Just as the binding of a person with shackles and the like proceeds by depending entirely upon theft which has become the seed [of that bondage], so too does it proceed according to the method previously explained.
According to the previously stated principle (see *Kiraṇa* 1.16ff),

since passion (*rāga*) and the other [afflictions] arise in the *pralayakevalin* with reference to the impurity (*mala*) that constitutes their state as bound souls (*paśu*), how can it be questioned here whether passion is the cause? Thus it is.
Therefore, its state of being an enjoyer and its body as the object of enjoyment arise from other causes.
For the state of being an enjoyer exists through the condition of being a bound soul (paśu), and the bondage of Māyā resides within the body;
the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth for the bound soul is established through karma.
Otherwise, this bondage consisting of the state of being an enjoyer and the act of enjoyment would not have been described.
Commentary:

From the impurity designated as *paśutva* (the state of being a bound soul), he possesses the status of an enjoyer; from *māyā*, his body [arises]; and from *karman* (action), there is further experience (*bhoga*), because actions themselves transform into the nature of pleasure and pain. Thus, direct causality is stated here, and not indirect causality through a succession of steps.
We shall demonstrate that all of this, being of the nature of illusion, is projected by karma. (ad Kir 3:7–8)
And it is stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*: "Bodies, objects, and organs [arise] from karma. [Quote:
Bodies, objects, and organs arise from karma.]
And: "By itself" (svayam) [in verse 1:13ab].
Otherwise, its experience, its state of being an experiencer, and its body would not have been specified. Thus, by this much, the category of the bound soul (paśu-padārtha) has been examined.
Now, for the sake of specifically examining the category of the noose (pāśa), Garuḍa asks a question by way of context:
"O Lord of Gods, that which has been described as action (karman) is the cause of bondage to experience."
The acquisition of karma occurs only when a body exists; at the time of creation, from where could the body have come?
Commentary:

Regarding the statement that "karma is the cause of experience," beginning with the words "this experience consisting of pleasure, pain, and so forth," the ellipsis [to be supplied] is that "it is not all-pervasive.

For, immediately after the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), at the time of the commencement of creation, the first experience of the body and so forth is held to arise from some specific cause alone.
It is not from karma;
for those [bodies] that arise at subsequent times have karma as their cause. As they say:
"The first body has its root in the purpose of the person (puruṣārtha), while the others are understood to have their root in karma."
"For the first body...
[The source is unknown. It is also quoted in the *Narasiṃhapurāṇa* (NarP).]

Here, the Blessed One spoke this established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Just as its impurity is beginningless, so too is its karma beginningless.
If this variety were not established as beginningless, by what cause would it arise?
Commentary:

For the existence of karma is established by the fact that the diversity of bodily experiences and so forth among persons cannot otherwise be accounted for at any time; and because scripture declares the diversity of births—such as those of beasts, deer, birds, reptiles, stationary beings, humans, and so on—even at the time of creation;
and because karma is proven to exist even during the great dissolution (mahāpralaya), it is established that the continuous succession of karma and bodies is beginningless.
[Quotation: In the *Kiraṇavṛtti*, the venerable Rāmakaṇṭha states:
"For [the case] of persons, in every respect..."
The existence of karma is established by the fact that otherwise the diversity of bodies and enjoyments would be inexplicable,
even at the time of the first creation.
Because of the scriptural testimony regarding the diversity of beasts, birds, wild animals, reptiles, stationary beings, humans, and so forth,
and because of the persistence of karma even during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*),
the continuum of the body of karma is beginningless in its flow.
"It is established" has been explained [in the *Siddhāntasārāvalivyākhyā* on VP 7,

And thus, since it is established by implication that even *mala* alone is prohibited from being the cause of the body here, it follows that the position—that the first body has its root in the purpose of the *puruṣa*—is utterly untenable; this is what is meant.
This very point is shown by the *sūtra* in order to conclude that this [bondage] is beginningless like a stream and to demonstrate that *māyā* is its substratum.
Therefore, karma is beginningless, and illusion (māyā) and existence (bhava) are likewise;
similarly, Śiva exists as the beginningless creator of the entire universe.
Commentary:

Thus, existence (bhava) bound by karma—consisting of the categories (tattvas) from Kalā down to the Earth, as well as the elements (bhūtas) and worlds (bhuvanas)—is of the nature of Māyā; and the karma being acquired is, in turn, bound by that [existence].
Since karma and existence are thus mutual causes for one another, their beginninglessness as a continuous flow is established.

Furthermore, because existence (*bhava*) is beginningless, its material cause (*upādāna*) must also be beginningless; and since karma is beginningless, its substratum (*adhikaraṇa*), which is Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*), must likewise be beginningless.

This is because actions such as agriculture are observed to be the means of refining Primordial Matter, whereas it is impossible for them to refine a self (*ātman*) as postulated by the Naiyāyikas and others, as that would entail the consequence of the self being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*).
And that which is the material cause of existence and the substratum of karma is *māyā*, which is established as beginningless.

Likewise, since existence (bhava), consisting of the body, the organs, and the world, is said to be beginningless by way of its continuous flow, it is established that its creator, the Lord (Īśvara), is also beginningless.
Now, following the specific examination of the category of "bonds" (pāśa), Garuḍa spoke a question for the purpose of examining the category of the "Lord" (pati) by way of a relevant digression:
Garuḍa said:
"O Lord, Śiva has been declared by you to be the creator; how is he to be known?

For only when God is established as the creator of the world can his beginninglessness be proven. Commentary: Indeed, once the Lord is established as the creator of the universe, it is possible to prove his beginninglessness.
How, then, is that very [self] known? It cannot be known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because you yourselves admit that it is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*).
As it has been said by the followers of Jaimini:
And this [Self] can never be known by anyone;
for [the scripture] would speak [of it] as the proof of the Self's sovereignty.

Even though [the Self] is perceived in its own essential nature, its status as a creator is not understood.
Nor is this conviction well-established by his word alone;
for he might speak even without having created [the world], since he could establish it through his own sovereign power.

Nor can it be established by inference—such as the perception of form and so forth, or the "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*) of the previously mentioned effects consisting of the body, the instruments, and the worlds—just as one infers the existence of the eyes and other senses; for [inference] observes that those [effects] arise from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) themselves.
As the Buddhists say: "When X exists, Y necessarily occurs; if one were to postulate something other than that [as the cause of Y]...
[yasminsati]

Because that [cause] would itself require a cause, there would be an infinite regress of causes in all cases.
Just as in the case of Caitra’s healing of a wound, [the agency] is attributed through connection with such things as weapons and medicines.
"Why is the causality of an unrelated post (sthāṇu) being postulated?
Nor can it be established by scripture, because you yourselves do not accept that [the world] is uncreated.
Because that which is produced by those [two] lacks validity due to mutual dependence,
and you have no other means of valid cognition;
the meaning is that, due to the absence of a means of valid cognition to establish that [other], it is not understood in any way whatsoever.
If this is so, then let there be doubt regarding this very object: "Does God not exist? Why? Because of the absence of any subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*). It is replied:
"How can agency be appropriate for one who is devoid of instruments and is formless? (Kir 3.9)
Commentary:
Lack of instruments is "instrumentlessness" (*vaikaraṇya*). Therefore, it is not possible for God to be the creator of the world.
Due to the absence of instruments, [He would be like] a potter who, being devoid of a staff, wheel, string, and so forth, could not produce a jar.
This has been stated by the followers of Jaimini:
"And no agent devoid of instruments creates anything whatsoever.
(Na ca niḥsādhanaḥ kartā kaścit sṛjati kiñcana).
Furthermore, corporeality is solidity.
In this context, because of the absence of such a body, it is impossible for God to be an agent;
for it has been stated by those very [authorities]:
"An unembodied controller would indeed be like a liberated soul."
"For the presiding agent must be bodiless; otherwise, the self would be like a liberated soul. (Śloka-vārttika 78cd). Also cited in the commentary on the *Narasiṃhapurāṇa*.

Thus, the prima facie position (*pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ*) is that the non-existence of God is established through the absence and presence of proving and refuting means of valid cognition (*sādhaka-bādhaka-pramāṇa*), as stated at 2:8, p. 130, and frequently in the *Mātṛkā-viniścaya*.

In this regard, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is preceded by the refutation of subverting factors (*bādhaka*). For as long as those are not refuted, the probative reason (*hetu*) simply does not function;
this is because the statement of that thesis (*pratijñā*) is itself subverted by inference (*anumāna*). As they have said:
"Because the statement of a reason applies when there is doubt, that which is excluded is not a locus for the reason. (Pramāṇavārttika)
4:91. Also quoted ad *Narada-purāṇa* 2:4, p. 119:
"In the same way, it is introduced:
the Blessed One said."
Just as time, though formless, is seen to bring about results,
so too Śiva, though formless, accomplishes his work by his will.
Commentary:

In this regard, the reason (hetu) stated for establishing non-agency—namely, "because of being formless" (amūrtatvāt)—is inconclusive (anaikāntika) with respect to time (kāla), since it is well-known that despite its being formless, time possesses agency in relation to flowers, fruits, and so forth.

Now, if it is argued that because time is insentient (acetana), it lacks agency toward its own effects due to its status as a mere instrumental cause (kāraṇatva), and thus the reason does not fall into the domain of being inconclusive; [we reply:]...

To this it is replied: In that case, because time here serves as a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to our own selves and others; for even though they are formless (*amūrta*), one observes effects such as the movement of their own bodies.

Furthermore, the example provided here is unestablished regarding the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma-asiddha*), because we also accept that the liberated self (*muktātman*) is the presiding controller of all.
Moreover, the reason stated here—"because of the absence of instruments" (*vaikaraṇyāt*)—is likewise unestablished. For instance:
His instrument is simply his will, as is held by those who possess immediate yoga.
Commentary: Since he possesses a power consisting solely of will, that very will serves as his instrument, just like that of a yogin.

Furthermore, yogins are established for all proponents of philosophical systems; even by the Cārvākas, they cannot be rejected, just like gems, medicinal herbs, and so forth, because they perform the healing of poison and seizures. As they say:
"The power of gems, mantras, and medicinal herbs is indeed inconceivable."
"For the power of jewels, mantras, and medicinal herbs is indeed inconceivable.
This also occurs in the *Ratnāvalī*, Act 2, p. 39, and in the *Śuklakurukullāsādhana*.

Alternatively, if the intended reason here is the absence of sense faculties (*indriya*), that too is addressed: "For a farmer is seen performing the extraction of a thorn even though he lacks [intact] eyes;
while his activity may not be visible, his desire for the task is nevertheless perceived. (KirT 3.11)
Commentary: At that time, the magnet stone (*ayaskāntamaṇi*) constitutes an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika-hetu*),
because it is observed to attract a body consisting of a thorn even though it is devoid of sense faculties (*indriya*).

In this case as well, the objection regarding the inconclusiveness [of the reason] based on time, as previously mentioned, and its refutation should be understood in exactly the same way. Thus, when the subverting proof that determines non-existence has been removed, a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is now stated to eliminate doubt regarding existence.
The gross, variegated effect cannot exist otherwise [than as produced];
therefore, there must be some cause.
(Vṛtti)
In this proof of the existence of God (Īśvara), the Sāṃkhyas, Buddhists, Jaiminīyas, Jainas, and Cārvākas are the opponents.

Among them, regarding the first two [schools], that which was previously stated as the world— the body, the instruments, the worlds, and so forth— which is variegated and has an unseen agent (adṛṣṭakartṛka) and is intended to be the subject (dharmin), is already established as an effect (kārya) because it undergoes transformation or arises at every moment.
But for others,
the world has never been otherwise than it is now.

Since [the opponent] accepts this, the world and so forth— which are parts of that [whole]— are not established as being such [i.e., non-composite]; therefore, for their sake, the state of being an effect is here proven by means of grossness.
Whatever is gross is an effect, such as a jar and so forth; and this world and its like are gross and have an unseen agent; therefore, they are effects.
Nor is there an inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) here due to the Lord’s eternal body or the Veda, as has been stated by the followers of Jaimini.
"And your reason would be inconclusive on account of that [person's] body and so forth. (Śloka-vārttika 77ab)
As quoted [ad *Nar* 2:8, p. 133 and ad *Mṛg* 1:9, p. 21]: "Because we accept that this [world] and the Veda are in every respect non-eternal;
and now, once that [Veda] has been established as an effect, it is being proved here that this entire world, by virtue of its being an effect, is preceded by an agent."
But it is not by way of grossness, because that [grossness] is pervaded by it.
Whatever is an effect cannot be established without an agent endowed with specific knowledge and action, just as in the case of a jar and so forth;
and this entire world is indeed an effect.
Therefore, that [the world] also cannot come into being without a creator endowed with specific knowledge and action;
and since he who is its creator is established as God (Īśvara), there is no contradiction here, as the three terms do not have redundant meanings.
Nor should it be suspected that "being an effect" (kāryatva) is not established in such a manner here.
As the Buddhists say:
"That which is established as following the presence or absence of a presiding agent...
[siddhaṃ yādṛgadhiṣṭhātṛ]
devdot hutāśane Pramāṇavārttika 1:13–14. Also quoted ad Mat VP.
That which is inferred from it—namely, its configuration and so forth—is endowed with that [quality]. (6:100, p. 227; and ad *Nar* 2:5, p. 122)
"It is not correct to infer [a specific thing] from that which is established as distinct in its actual entity, merely because of a similarity of words,
just as one cannot infer fire from a white substance.

This is because the pervasion of the mere effect by the mere agent is established in the case of a jar and so forth, just as the mere state of being produced is pervaded by the mere state of impermanence.

Otherwise, if one were to postulate a difference in the reason (hetu) based on a difference between the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) and the example (dṛṣṭānta), even in those cases and elsewhere, there would be a total absence of all inference.

[Otherwise] it would follow that [the world] has as its creator one who is not a Lord (anīśvara), is subject to destruction, and so forth. (See 3:1, p. 101; ad *Nar* 2:7, p. 128, and frequently in the *Mātṛvṛtti*.)
Because there is an absence of negative pervasion (*viparyayavyāpti*).

"In the world, parts of chariots and the like, though fashioned by various carpenters,

For example, Kir. 2:14d and the commentary thereon:
"Now, [I shall explain] the essential nature of *anantādi*."
He is omniscient, possesses a pure body, and is the illuminator of all knowledge.
Commentary: The meaning is that this [individual soul] is deficient from Īśvara only in respect to the power of agency (kartṛtva), but not even in respect to the power of knowledge (jñatva).
And his body is pure, not impure like that of one who holds office within the womb of *māyā*.
He stands as the instructor of all the Śiva-knowledges, divided into ten and eighteen varieties, and not merely of a few, like other gurus.
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Śrīmatkiraṇavṛtti*, composed by Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha, the son of Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha.
Now, another section follows by way of a question for the purpose of examining in detail the very subject matter of the investigation.
Garuḍa said:
"By the power of Śiva’s Śakti, Ananta indeed awakens."
And that power, which awakens [all], is recited as being omnipresent.
Why does it not produce cognition even for others who are in close proximity?
If [you argue] that it assists only those who are fit, then Śiva would be subject to passion. (KirT 4.2)
Commentary: Here, the word-meanings, context, and connections of the sūtra are to be understood as before;
however, the sequence of the discussion consists specifically of a detailed examination immediately following the analysis of the categories.
But that which consists of speech is said to be manifold, such as "the infinite," "the lord," and "the dark one" (asite), and so forth.
And this is the meaning of the question here:
it has been stated that "the group beginning with Ananteśa is awakened by His power" (*tacchaktipratibodhitaḥ*).

Furthermore, because the power of Īśvara is all-pervasive and thus present everywhere, there would be no distinction [between individuals]; consequently, all selves would possess the nature of Ananta and the other [emanations], or else none at all would.

If it is argued that he acts [to bestow such states] in consideration of the fitness for service and so forth, then, due to his connection with attachment, aversion, and the like in performing that act, the consequence follows that he would be non-Īśvara, just like an ordinary person.
On this point, the Blessed One spoke the established conclusion:
"Is the awakening of a lotus not indeed equal [to its opening] through contact with the rays of the sun?"
Some awaken, while others never do so at all.
Passion and hatred do not exist in the sun, nor do they exist in the Lord, because He has no [personal] purpose;
His activity proceeds from His office, for there is no persistence [of activity] without such an office.
"By virtue of that power, O Bird, Ananta would possess omniscience.
Commentary:
True; the pervasive power is also supportive by depending upon [the recipient's] capacity.

Nor can passion and hatred be inferred from that [state], because such a state is not established here for those who possess the qualification; for here, the qualification of the eligible persons consists in the ripeness of their impurity, which is their fitness.
It is said that for those whose impurities are ripened, that [state] bestows awakening.

Just as one who is capable of being awakened is awakened by the Sun, so too, because of that qualification characterized by capability, there is the command of the Infinite One; for it has been stated that without such a command, the establishment of external effects is not possible.

Nor is it established that such a pursuit of capability is invariably concomitant with passion, hatred, and the like; therefore, the consequence of [the Lord] being non-omniscient does not follow from this.
Now, right here, there is another question for examination.
Garuḍa said:
"If a body exists, omniscience is not possible for Ananta."
Since the sense-faculties (*akṣa*) are fixed and their respective objects of apprehension are also fixed.
*Vṛtti*:
As for what was stated—that [the Buddha] is omniscient, possesses a pure body, and is infinite—that is not tenable.

The meaning is as follows: since, according to the reasoning previously stated, the connection with a body characterized by the performance of specific functions is pervaded by being a specific perceiver—and this is established as residing in all embodied beings—therefore, the negation of omniscience is made through the perception of a property incompatible with [the subject's] nature as an embodied being (*śarīritva*).

Now, an objection is raised: "This reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), because the body and its instruments are distinct [from the Self], and it has been stated that the Infinite [Self] possesses a pure body. To this, it is replied:
That body, consisting of illusion, is born from the cause of residual karma.
Even if there were indeed a distinction, such as the ability to hear from a great distance and so forth;
[the *Vṛtti* states:

first of all, it is not possible for that body to possess purity—either by being non-illusory in nature or by not being born of karma—because it is a body, just like the bodies of ourselves and others. As they have said:
"The claim that there is the existence of a body above [the realm of] illusion is merely a pleasant rumor."
Verses with the same concluding formula appear in *Nyāyamañjarī*, Vol.
1, p. 81 (verse 84d) and p. 91 (verse 104d).
If, on the other hand, [the body] is indeed produced by specific karma—just like the bodies of Brahmā and others—then this must be stated.
And consequently, through its connection with such a body, its excellence, such as hearing from a great distance, would be established just like theirs. As they say:
"Whatever excellence is observed in one case, that very same excellence occurs elsewhere through the power of leaping."* (*This refers to the analogy of a person who can leap further by training.)
"The [capacity] that is observed as a specific excellence in one case is the very same [that is transferred] elsewhere through leaping;
however, omniscience is not such [a capacity]. Therefore, this reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*). This is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
On this point, the established conclusion is as follows:
The Blessed One said, "His body is said to consist of pure origins and is not born of karma. (KirT 4.7)
Since he is thus liberated from the bonds, by what could his knowledge be obstructed? Commentary:
Here, the pervasion [of the self] by the nature of *māyā* in the body is unestablished.
It has been stated that [Śiva] is also possible as the self of pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyātman*), as in the passage beginning with "In the pure path, Śiva is the agent" (Kiraṇa 3.26c).
For this very reason, that [omniscience] is not born of karma, because it is the substratum of *māyā*, and karma is impossible therein;
rather, it is based solely on its [the Lord's] sovereign authority (*adhikāra*).
Since He, who is infinite, has been thus liberated from the bonds consisting of *māyā* in the manner described, who could possibly obstruct His omniscience? Thus, there is no contradiction.

Or, let it be granted that even the womb of purity possesses the nature of a bond because it is to be severed by initiation; nevertheless, just as the snake residing within it does not harm the poison located therein, so too [the bond] does not afflict that which resides within it.
In this way, the accumulation of bonds residing within it does not afflict the infinite [Self].
Commentary:
For just as the poison of a snake, even though situated within its own body, [does not harm the snake that emits it]...
Or, just as that which has been transferred from within another serpent does not cause harm by virtue of being poison, so it is for Ananta.
That [power] residing in the locus of its realization is of the nature of Śuddhavidyā, because it is implied by the agency of Śuddhavidyā which brings about the body and other such effects.
The accumulation of bonds consisting of the body is not an obstacle;
thus, it is stated that even those such as Vīrabhadra, who hold office within the womb of Māyā, are not afflicted by the accumulation of the bonds of Māyā.
This has been said by the Gurus:
Even when engaged with the *kalās*, we are not subject to them like a herd of bound souls;
for we are beyond them.
"Those [energies] are subject to them along with the bound souls (paśus); therefore, they are above them.
If this is so, then since even Śuddhavidyā is severed from the Lord Ananta as a bond (pāśa), just like other bonds, how can this accumulation of bonds consist of the body?
To this it is replied: Just as that which is cut off and born again from what has been cut off may occur by virtue of its dependence on a particular location. // KirT_4.9 //
By means of the yoga of abiding, the Lord of Mantras maintains the body like a *haṭha* plant.
Commentary: Just as the *gaḍūcī* plant, though severed from its root, takes refuge in a particular location and grows anew.

In this way, even though Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā) has been severed, it attains a new growth by resorting to a specific locus characterized by its authority over Ananta, taking on the nature of his body and so forth; thus, by the power of that authority, Ananteśa maintains a body as if by force, even though he is without desire— there is no contradiction here.
Furthermore, that inference which was stated regarding the body being born of karma is also said to be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*):
"Just as a body remains supported for a long time through the power of mantras. (KirT 4.10)
Even one bitten by the serpent of Time attains his desired state through the power [of the mantra];
for it is by the efficacy of that power that his body remains thus.
Therefore, the body should be known as utterly stainless, like a lotus leaf.
Commentary: One who is bitten by a serpent at the very moment of death is "bitten by Time" (*kāladaṣṭa*); the meaning is that his karma is exhausted.

Just as his body, sustained by the power of a mantra alone, remains for a long time and reaches the desired place through the power of that very person previously mentioned— whose nature consists of knowledge and action— so too, by the efficacy of the Lord’s power known as *adhikāra* (sovereign authority), the body of Ananteśa is indeed not born of karma.
"Therefore, by that previous reasoning and by the characteristics of the *kārma* and *māyīya* [bodies],
it should be known to be untouched by impurities, like a lotus leaf by water.

By this, it is stated that the reason "because of being a body" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) here, since we observe that even for some of us [ordinary beings], there are bodies not born of karma (*akarmaja*).

Now, one might object: "Since his body is a locus of awakening, just like that of people such as ourselves, why is it said that he 'maintains his body by force' (haṭhāt)? It is for this purpose [the following is stated]:
"Just as the nutrient essence (rasa) within the body is rendered wholesome and effective when assisted by the vital principles (tantras). (KirT 4.12)
In that same way, the immensely powerful consciousness abides within this body.
Commentary:

Just as mercury (pārada), which is excellent for processing and movement, is extremely unstable in the body, yet is assisted by other substances—such as those used in the Tantras for maintaining its family and so forth—it becomes fit for its purpose.

While that body remains, even though consciousness is supported by the tantras— which consist of the power of the will of Ananteśa, the Lord— and is possessed of great strength, it is nonetheless limited in its objects within the body due to the state of having severed impurities.

This is what is meant: a body is assumed for the manifestation of consciousness by those whose impurities are uninterrupted, but not by those whose impurities are severed, even though they rely upon the principle of Īśvara; thus it has been emphatically stated that Ananta does not maintain a body for the sake of assisting his consciousness.
Is this [body] then entirely useless to him?
It is said: "No;
for example, through the power of medicine, strength becomes supreme even for those who were powerless. (Kir 4.13)
By the power and efficacy of that [consciousness], it enters into the supreme strength of the Infinite;
through that application of power, it impels the womb in an instant.
Vṛtti:

Just as for those who are powerless, power increases through the efficacy of medicinal herbs and the like, so too, by means of the power inherent in that body, there arises the capacity to establish agency; from that, the strength of Ananteśa consists in the conjunction with the object to be refined (*saṃskārya*) and other such functions within the supreme *śivatattva*.

The meaning is this: even though he possesses omniscience, because his agency is inferior to that of Śiva due to the influence of *kalā*, the operations of purifying, joining, and so forth are not possible for him here; therefore, a body must necessarily be employed—just as in the case of people like us—in order to manifest even that portion of agency, and thus there is no fault.
Regarding this very point, a question is raised for the sake of further examination.
Garuḍa said:
What is the use of a driver for that which is already impelled on the lower path? In this world, Māyā is subject to transformation by its own inherent modification. (KirT 4.15)

Since the world-source is said to consist of its modifications such as *kalā* and the rest, and since total destruction would follow from modification, how could the world not be a modification? (KirT 4.16)

Commentary: Now, this question is indeed untenable, because it has already been refuted by logic (*nyāya*) in the previous establishment of God (*īśvara*); and the resolution has also already been stated before, namely: "If it is argued that action cannot belong to the insentient."
"If karma were [the agent], it would not be insentient" (Kir. 3.12d).
Now, the question is: what need is there for an impeller other than that which is to be impelled?
That [position] as well is indeed untenable, because it has been refuted by the passage beginning with "Just as by the Lord of the Earth-circle" (*yathā bhūmaṇḍaleśena*).
Nor is it appropriate to explain that there is here a further objection against the Lord from the perspective of the Sāṃkhya;
for the refutation of even that view was already possible through the earlier [statement] beginning with "the effect is gross and variegated. (Quote:
"The effect is gross and variegated...")
For if that were impossible, another question would indeed be appropriate, but not otherwise, as it would lead to the undesirable consequence [of questioning] even the *kalās* and so forth.

To this it is replied: This very point accepted here—that the absence of Īśvara is being established—is the meaning of the question, specifically with reference to the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*).

For at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), since Ananta and the others have been withdrawn and the Blessed Lord remains in a state of peace alone, having set aside his states as Īśvara and so forth, there being no external impeller, Māyā— by virtue of being the source of the universe— is accepted as undergoing transformation through its own inherent nature into increasingly subtle states, becoming fit for the manifestation of its effects; likewise, at the time of the commencement of creation, [she transforms] into the form of the effects beginning with *kalā*.
If it is argued that [the world] will come to be, what is the use of postulating a mover for it?

Furthermore, if even then the withdrawal of the mover is not admitted, there follows the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga-viparyaya) that a great dissolution (mahāpralaya) would be impossible because there would be no distinction [between the states].

Moreover, since Māyā is subject to modification, if it were partless, it would follow that at the time of the effect it would be destroyed through transformation in its entirety, like milk turning into curds.
For if it [Prakṛti] were composed of parts, then, like a jar or other objects, it would be preceded by a cause, and thus its status as the ultimate cause would be lost.

Alternatively, if modification is not admitted for it, then, because it would lack the nature of a material cause (*upādāna*), there would be no production of the world. Such is the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*) based on these two undesirable consequences. Here follows the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The Blessed One said:
Because it is insentient, that [prakṛti] is impelled by the purpose of the Puruṣa as its cause;
since there is no modification from its own side, its impeller is therefore infinite.

Commentary: Even during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), by virtue of being for the sake of the *puruṣa*, [the Lord] impels [the principles] directly, according to the manifestation of the *kalās* and so forth, through various states such as subtle and subtler.
The meaning is that even then, because the state of the Lord and so forth is not withdrawn, the aforementioned undesirable consequence does not arise.
As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"Even during sleep, he remains [active], awakening those fit for awakening, restraining those fit for restraint, ripening the karma of those under the influence of karma,
making manifest the powers of *māyā* that are ready for manifestation, and perceiving every category of entity exactly as it is."
"Even during sleep,
the collection of objects remains [in consciousness]," as quoted in the *Mṛgendratantra-vṛtti* (VP) 4.15, and also cited in the *Nareśvaraparīkṣā*.
And the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) is the withdrawal of the external effects, beginning with the *kalās*.
For it has been stated that therein Ananta and the others possess the agency.
Nor does the second undesirable consequence (*prasanga*) follow; this is what is being said.
Just as the ocean, due to the force of the wind, undergoes transformation only on its surface,
so too Māyā, because of its immovability, remains subject to modification through the categories beginning with Kalā.
Commentary: Just as the ocean undergoes a transformation in the form of waves through only certain limited powers and not by all its powers,
so too Māyā— because it consists of a collection of powers— undergoes transformations such as *kalā* and the rest through only a few of its powers.
"It is not by all [the powers] because of its immovability (*akṣobhyatva*).
Here, the opponent's intention is:
"If it is not agitated (*akṣubdha*), it cannot be a producer of effects."
Commentary:

Since even the powers that have undergone transformation possess the same state of coexistence as those that have not, it would be impossible for them to undergo further transformation in the absence of agitation; consequently, the production of effects would be impossible.
Therefore, one must necessarily admit that all [powers] are agitated. Thus, the reason "because of being unshakeable" (*akṣobhyatvāt*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) in this context.
Here is the established conclusion:
agitation is its movement;
that power, impelled by him, becomes eternally effective in producing effects. (KirT 4.19)
Commentary: This general agitation, which consists of impulsion and pertains to all powers, is indeed admitted [to exist].
However, this specific agitation, which consists of an effect, belongs to only a certain power.
And thus it is said that there is no lack of proof here:
"The aforementioned Akṣobhyā, by virtue of her omnipresence, stands as the cause of the world;
like Māyā, she pervades everything, yet the multitude of her effects does not [fully] occupy the path."
Having pervaded all entities beginning with the kalās, she remains unshaken; therefore, she is remembered as Akṣobhyā.
Commentary:
By virtue of her omnipresence—that is, by her nature as possessing all powers—she is not agitated by being an effect; thus she is described as "Imperturbable" (Akṣobhya).
She is inferred through her nature as the cause of the world.
Because they arise as Akṣobhya himself in that form, the *bhāvas*—namely *kalā* and the others—are of the nature of his effects; he abides pervading them.

The meaning is that their origination occurs within his very womb according to the analogy of the "ghee-worm" (*ghṛtakīṭa*), and not because they are produced by his state of being (*tadbhāvabhāvitvāt*).
In the world, it is observed that for an effect such as a jar, the cause is the substance itself, such as clay, and not its power (*śakti*).
Why, then, is it said that "power (śakti) is the producer of the effect"? To this it is replied: That power which produces the effect is called action (kriyā), and it has a subtle form.
Even though it is subtle, it abides within gross effects, like the seed of a banyan tree.

Commentary: Even in the world, just like the seed of a *nyagrodha* tree, even a subtle power (*śakti*) that effects its gross effect is established as being denoted by the term "transformation" (*pariṇati*), having as its substrate a property that is eternally inferable;
however, it is not the case that the substance lacks power even in its state of potentiality.
Because of its existence; as they say:
"The causal factor (*kāraka*) is power (*śakti*), not substance (*dravya*), because of deviation."

It has been well said that "power is the producer of the effect," because even when an incapable thing is joined with auxiliary causes, its effect is not observed due to the absence of those auxiliaries.
What, then, is said in the present context?
