Therefore, she should be known as the cause of this gross [universe] in its entirety.
Commentary: Thus it has been stated that although Māyā possesses many powers, she does not transform through the nature of all her powers simultaneously.

For that reason, it is stated that a certain power of this [Prakṛti] is the cause of the entire effect, such as the gross elements and so forth; however, it is not a separate power. Thus, the second objection is also untenable. Now, what is the direct cause of the entire world?
It is said: "No;
therefore, *kalā* is established as *tuṭi*, for it is the awakener that creates desire. (KirT 4.22)

Subtler than these [gross elements] are the qualities; from them arises intellect (*buddhi*), and from intellect, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkṛti*). From that [ego-sense] arise the eleven organs and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*); from those, the gross elements are born. The Lord creates all this below.
Commentary: From that principle of Māyā, Kalā, Tuṭi, Time (Kāla), and Saṃsthā—previously mentioned—are produced directly, as is Niyati itself.
As it is stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*:
Therefore, [it is said]: "O Kālakalā.
(Svayam 2:9a; cf. Sadyojāta).
Interpretation (p. 43):
"Kalā ca kalā ca" is an *ekaśeṣa* compound [meaning "part and part"]. "Kālaśca kalā ca" is [the compound] "kālakale" [meaning "time and parts"].
In that context, one word "kalā" denotes necessity (niyati), while the second denotes a digit (kalā) itself.
How so? Regarding the word "kalā":
It designates *niyati* (destiny),
because it too apportions and impels; it is called *niyati* by virtue of being the distributor of the fruits of karma.
In that context, by the word *kalā*, *niyati* (restriction) is also included.
*Bodhanī*, however, is the aforementioned *vidyā* (knowledge).
As for the word *hi* (for), because [avidyā] has arisen from that cause, therefore the aforementioned *rāga* (attachment) is produced by desire (*abhilāṣa*).
And that subtle *pradhāna*, previously described as having the qualities (*guṇa*) as its cause, arises from that very source;
it does not arise from *māyā* because of the indication of a different sequence, but rather from *kalā* itself, which was mentioned previously in the sequence of the effects.
As it is said in the venerable *Raurava*:
From the principle of *kalā*, the two principles of *rāga* and *vidyā* came into being,
as well as the *avyakta*.
Regarding the phrase "and the unmanifest," from that principle—
the *pradhāna*— which is denoted by the subtle term "that" (*ataḥ*), there arise the three qualities (*guṇa*), namely *sattva* and the others; from those qualities, the intellect (*buddhi*) arises.

It has already been shown previously that this is a restatement (anuvāda) for the purpose of grasping specific varieties of entities such as the principles (tattvas), which are well-known from general treatises like the *Buddhi* and so forth.
And it has been stated by the Sāṃkhyas: "From primordial nature (prakṛti) comes the Great One (mahat); from that, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra); and from that, the group of sixteen."
From primordial nature arises the Great One (mahat); from that, the I-principle (ahaṃkāra), and from that, the five elements. (Sāṃkhyakārikā 22)
Therefore, from those five among the sixteen, the five gross elements [arose].
"All" refers to that which consists of the elements, their states, and the worlds.
He also created the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), which is situated below and composed of the gross elements. Thus it is.
Thus the Blessed Lord Īśa, endowed with Śiva-śakti, created [the world].
2:11c, and /RauS/ 1:12d and /Svayam/ 2:10d.
The entire effect, consisting of pure, impure, and mixed [elements], is of the nature of illusion.
Commentary: All this [universe] was created by that very Ananteśa through the medium of Māyā;
it is the substratum, interspersed with both pure and impure subjects.
The meaning is that they too were created by him alone;
as it is stated in the venerable *Raurava*:
"The Lords are both beyond *añjana* and possessed of *añjana*, of various kinds."
And the *pata* paintings, transcending collyrium, are established [there].
(Rauravaśāsana 2:20; the edition reads *vāpi* instead of *devās*)
"In every world, the gods are established by his command.
Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, he created that which is pure, impure, and mixed, even in its own essential nature (svarūpa).
As it has been stated by the Sāṃkhyas:
The creation is vast with *sattva* at the top and vast with *tamas* at the root.
"Furthermore, in the middle [of this], the world-system is vast with its constituent elements (rajas), extending from Brahmā down to a blade of grass (stamba).
This is the opponent's position regarding this point.
[The world] is born from the womb [of Māyā], and because of the diversity of intellects; if that [source] is one, how can it be twofold?
Commentary: The "womb" is Māyā; since everything is non-distinct by virtue of being produced from her, it is all indeed [one].
The body of the pure ones is pure;
the world itself would likewise be pure.
The meaning is that it is of one form alone.
Furthermore, how could he have created it in two ways—as somewhat impure, or as impure, or as mixed?
Because such a thing is impossible, as they say:
There is no appropriation of that which is contradictory.
{Direct Perception Section} 263c.
Now, this pair is differentiated from the one as its modes,
just as from rice there arise boiled rice and cakes.
"Therefore, no contradiction between these two is possible.
To this it is said: "Because of the difference in cognition" (*buddhibhedāt*).
For when there is a difference in cognition, the duality of food, such as boiled rice and so forth, exists by virtue of being the modes (*prakāra*) of that [cognition].
But for that which, when there is no difference in cognition from a single [instance], does not possess multiplicity, it does not become twofold by way of being a mode of that [cognition],
as a jar [does] by way of its absence; and yet,
there is multiplicity when there is a difference in cognition.
From the previously mentioned impure [state] comes the pure, and from the pure comes the impure.
Therefore, how could that [impurity] also be twofold by way of being a mode of that [purity]? It is certainly not so.
Since there is no difference in their mode of being, here there is indeed a difference between entities, just as in the case of a jar and its absence.
Therefore, it is entirely appropriate to ask why the substratum (*upādāna*) is not contradictory [to its own absence].
However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:
That [difference] is observed in the case of fireflies and so forth, and it is produced by a single cause, which is contradictory [to your position].
Commentary: This is incorrect because it is unestablished; for indeed...

We do not maintain that the state of being a different kind [of cause] for a different kind [of effect] constitutes a different kind [of cause] itself, based on a difference in cognition regarding it;
rather, it is because the possessor of the mode (the substrate) is perceived as such.

For instance, although there is a difference in cognition regarding fireflies, mosquitoes, flies, and so forth—based on whether they possess the nature of light or lack it—there is no difference in cognition regarding them as being born from the same source, namely sweat; thus, their status as modes of that [source] is observed.

Similarly, in this case, although there is a distinction between the pure and the impure due to the difference in intellect (*buddhi*) consisting of knowledge and ignorance, because there is no difference in intellect regarding their being born from a womb (*yonija*), it is logical that they are divided into two types solely by way of their specific modes (*prakāra*). Thus, even though the various modes are characterized by mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihāravirōdha*), the fact that they share a single material cause (*upādāna-hetutva*)—as seen in the case of fireflies, mosquitoes, flies, and so forth—is not contradictory; therefore, there is no fault. To explain further:
Thus, that which possesses a different configuration, joined with pure and impure components,
should be known as the effect arising from the power of the cause, born from the seed as its instrumental condition.
(Vṛtti)

Thus, although they share the same cause—the power of the seed-syllable (*ekabīja*) as the source—those situated in the pure, impure, and immeasurable categories should be understood as having different configurations due to their different modes;
it is not by way of absolute difference, like a jar and its absence.
Now follows the conclusion of the present topic.
Thus has this been commanded; that task, which relies upon the body, must now be performed.
Commentary:

In this analysis, that which has the subtle body as its substratum within this gross body—namely, the effects of Māyā such as *kalā* and so forth—is designated by the Supreme Lord as the "subtle body. How so? It is explained as follows:
Although these effects are mutually contradictory and of a non-existent nature,
nevertheless, they are clearly and perfectly integrated within a single reality.
One should accomplish the distinct purpose of the individual (nara), just as the parts of a man’s chariot [function together].
Vṛtti:
Although this impure manifestation of Māyā, beginning with *kalā*, is mutually exclusive in nature—like a jar and its absence—and is thus opposed to that [pure state],...

Nevertheless, it is conceivable that this [nature], being closely joined to the single entity of the subtle body, makes its purpose for the person manifest and accomplishes it through the various operations of *kalā* and the rest—aided by the previously mentioned reinforcement of consciousness—just as the parts of a cart, when joined to the cart, accomplish their respective functions. Thus, this basis of the body has been created by the Infinite One. (Kirātārjunīya 4.28)
Commentary:

Since this [body] is thus the means for accomplishing the goals of the person (*puruṣārtha*), for that reason it is "bound to the body," meaning its stability is dependent upon the body; as the support of the gross body, it was created by Ananteśa as a means for accomplishing the goals of the person, and not otherwise.
Now, what is this human goal (puruṣārtha), and how is it bound to the body? It is said:
"There is no liberation without the body, nor is there experience, which is the weight of the activity of consciousness.
(Vṛtti)

In that regard, liberation and experience are the two goals of the person (puruṣārtha), for the teacher instructs consciousness and activity through experience— since they are not instructed without experience, as in states such as dissolution or isolation (pralayakevala). And this [instruction] is not possible without a body.
For liberation is not possible without the ripening of impurities, according to the principle that "that which is unmixed does not undergo transformation.
And since such ripening is impossible for it [the soul] in isolation, it has been stated that there must necessarily be a dependence on a body, as that [ripening] occurs concomitantly with it.
Since enjoyment is also observed to have no activity without a substratum for these means of enjoyment, its dependence upon a body is well-established; thus there is no contradiction.
Not only is the agent here infinite, but Śambhu performs this [action] as well, due to his autonomy and sovereignty.
It is all-encompassing and peaceful; by its power, the entire fruit [of action] is realized.
Commentary: The word "and" (*ca*) here is placed out of its logical order; it signifies that the Supreme Lord performs that [action] and not Ananteśa alone.
The meaning is that both possess the status of agent here through the relationship of the instigator and the one being instigated.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the commentary on the venerable *Kiraṇa*, composed by Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha, the son of Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha.
Now begins another section, preceded by a question, for the purpose of further examination of the category of "bond" (pāśa).
Garuḍa said:
Initiation arises from the descent of power (śaktipāta); the descent does not occur through [the Guru's] omnipotence.
Vṛtti:
In this regard, the meaning of the words of the sūtra, the context, and the connection should be understood as before.
However, when one has been initiated by a Guru through the descent of intense power (*tīvra-śakti-nipāta*), which consists of the [sacred] utterance (*vākya*):
It is of many kinds, as indicated by such passages as: "When one is initiated by a Guru through the descent of intense power" (Kirana-tantra 1.21ab).
But the *pāṭalika* is one who favors all and is peaceful, and so forth; as it is said:
"He who favors all is peaceful" (*sarvānugrāhakaḥ śāntaḥ*, *Kiraṇa* 4.29c).
And this is the meaning of the question here:
that which was stated—that one is initiated by the descent of the intense power—is incorrect.

For "descent" (pāta) is established as being pervaded by non-pervasiveness, as in the case of a jujube fruit in a bowl; and since pervasiveness is the opposite of that, then here, through the perception of what is opposed to pervasiveness, there is an absence of non-pervasiveness in the power by virtue of its being pervasive.
The absence of falling is what is being established;
nor is this reason unestablished,
for that power which awakens is recited as being omnipresent.
"And that power is recited as being all-pervading and awakening" (Kir.
4:1cd), because its omnipresence has already been accepted previously.
But it is not said that there is uncertainty here due to illusion,
because [the power] resides inherently in Śiva and thus exists eternally within the bound soul (paśu).
Commentary:
It has been stated that Māyā is the insentient power residing in Parigraha.
Consequently, because its nature is transformation (pariṇati), it is logical to say that after the dissolution of the person (puruṣa), she descends through the sequence of effects.

But this [consciousness], because it is inherent in the Supreme Lord, has the nature of non-transformation due to its being of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*). As it has been said: "Transformation is possible for the insentient, but it is not applicable to the sentient.
(pariṇāmo 'cetanasya cetanasya na yujyate)

And therefore, since [the power] always exists in the sacrificial animal as being characterized by grace (*sānugrāhikatva*), there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) because the reason has been qualified by the condition "while being inherent" (*samavetatve sati*); this is the meaning here.
Now, if that very state is called "falling" (*pāta*). If this is so—
Since the power [of bondage] exists eternally, why would there not be a cessation of worldly existence?
Commentary:

Because that power resides in all persons and is established as beginningless, liberation for all persons would likewise be beginningless due to their connection with initiation (*dīkṣā*); thus, there follows the undesirable consequence of the non-existence of *saṃsāra*.
Even granting the existence of power, the aforementioned downfall is stated;
or else it is time [that causes it], but what is that time said to be? If it is time, then what is its use for Śiva?
Commentary: The word "vā" (or) is intended to indicate the acceptance of an alternative position.
Or rather, as was stated previously:
"When a similar action has arisen by virtue of the power of a different time.
(Kir. 1.20cd)
The time for the ripening of impurities has been declared;
by the word "and" (ca), it is asked what else has been declared.
The meaning is: is it only the previously mentioned time for the descent of power (śaktipāta), or is it something else?

However, it should not be explained as being [the object] of that very [consciousness] in its state of being unknown, because, as has been established previously, ignorance is impossible for that [consciousness].
Furthermore, the claim previously stated— that time is the cause of the descent of power (śaktipāta), and the descent of power is the cause of initiation (dīkṣā)— is also untenable.

The meaning of the question is as follows: If time is accepted as the cause of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), then let that alone be the cause of initiation (*dīkṣā*); what is the use here of postulating Śiva as the cause of liberation by way of the descent of power?
As for worldly experience (*bhoga*), since it has been established [in the text] by the statement beginning with "the effect is gross and manifold," let time itself be its agent.
*{sthūlaṃ vicitrakaṃ kāryam}* (The effect is gross and manifold).
The Blessed One spoke, gradually resolving this series of questions: [Kir 3:12a].
In this world, the application of words is seen to occur through figurative usage;
for example, the omnipresent Self (puruṣa), though eternal and non-perishing, is spoken of as "going. (Kirātārjunīya 5.3)
Just as the severing of the bonds was described as the Lord Śiva, the King of Mantras,
so too is the descent of power (śaktinipāta) described by way of metaphorical convention.
Commentary:
Regarding that which was stated—that the descent [of grace] is not due to omnipresence but rather due to power—that is merely proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

For this very reason, because it is sublated by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) you have mentioned, we too accept that the scriptural passages concerning the "descent of power" (*śaktipāta*) possess a figurative meaning (*upacaritārtha*), since their primary sense is impossible.
Just as a person, though endowed with eternal and all-pervading attributes, is metaphorically said to be a "goer" and "perishable" by virtue of his body;
and just as the non-functioning of nooses toward a person who has undergone initiation is called "cutting," even though there is no actual physical splitting into two parts.

And just as he "shines by means of mantras" (*mantrair virājate*), he is called the "King of Mantras" (*mantrarāṭ*); thus, although the Blessed Lord is the Supreme Sovereign (*parameśvara*), he is spoken of [as such] through metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), and there is no contradiction.
Now, regarding the cause for this metaphorical designation, it is said concerning the sudden descent of the beginningless power of *Vāmā*:
"Just as the sudden fall of an object would be terrifying, so too is the descent [of this power]."
In the same way, even the descent of a thunderbolt is said to bring about the fear of worldly existence.
Therefore, just as [a stone] falls elsewhere, so too does the self [fall] toward the teacher.
Vṛtti:

For just as the falling of stones and such things causes fear to men, even so the beginningless connection with the power of the Supreme Lord is called a "fall" because it is the cause of the fear of saṃsāra.
Even for one connected to the power of Jyeṣṭhā, the previously mentioned downfall— occurring prior to initiation— is stated as a basis for metaphorical designation,
just as a teacher might wake sleeping students from the front with a staff.
Śiva too awakens those sleeping in the sleep of delusion by means of his power;
when the realization of one's own true nature occurs, it is then said that [the soul] has fallen [into grace].
Therefore, there must be the application of power (*śaktinipāta*), and that application signifies a mark (*cihna*).
Commentary:

Just as a teacher, even though all his students are equally positioned before him, strikes only those who are worthy and capable of instruction with a staff, and not those who are not his students; so too [is it here].

Thus, *moha* (delusion) is the impurity (*mala*); its effect is sleep, which is an incapacity regarding one's tasks—a specific state of ripening. Even when that [sleep] exists, the Supreme Lord awakens those who are asleep—those devoid of the consciousness of the means for its cessation—by means of that very power previously established.

In this way, when that same [power], according to the fitness of the ripening of the impurity, generates the specific knowledge of the means for its cessation through the sequence of dispassion toward worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) and so forth, then it is the power *Jyeṣṭhā* acting as the cause of the effect.
She is called "fallen" by way of metaphorical designation. As it has been said:
"Having brought about the suppression of its power, one acts free from desire for existence.
(kṛtvā tacchaktisaṃrodhaṃ kriyate bhavaniḥspṛhaḥ)
In the venerable Mataṅga[-tantra] as well, it is said:
"He, having destroyed all impurities, shall always become dispassionate toward saṃsāra."
"He would become dispassionate toward saṃsāra, with his impurities forever destroyed" (MatVP 10.25cd).
This is also stated in the venerable Svāyambhuva [Tantra].
From that union, his impurity— the cause of saṃsāra— is discharged;
[this leads] toward supreme liberation.
"When that [ignorance] has been destroyed, there arises the desire to go toward the supreme, ultimate good. Thus [it is said].
And therefore, as for what was said:
"Since the power [of the cause] exists at all times, why does the destruction of worldly existence not occur? (sthitatvāt sarvadā śakter bhavocchittir na kiṃ bhavet).
That too is indeed not a refutation;

for even though it exists at all times, it becomes the cause for the cessation of existence only at that specific time and place, in accordance with the ripening of the impurities there, and not at any other time or place.
The third question is also refuted:
"The time for that conjunction is the very same as that of the actions. (KirT 5.8)
Commentary: As it was said, "Or is it time? And what is that said to be? (kālo vā sa ca kaḥ proktaḥ).
Regarding this, it is said there: "And the very equality of karmas.
By the word *ca* (and), or by the word *tu* (but) acting in the place of *ca*, the previously mentioned ripening of impurity (*malaparipāka*) is also included.

By the word *eva* (only) here, the non-existence of a third time is stated; this is not because of the restriction [implied by] the previously mentioned [word], since that is a restrictive term used in conjunction [with another].

We shall demonstrate in the passage "the portion of karma which is greater is experienced first" that the word *tulya* (equal) has a dual sense, indicating both the equality of the two actions and the intensity of their ripening.
For at that time, whichever portion of karma was previously more potent in yielding its fruit, [that alone manifests].
(Kir. 5.10cd) Indeed, then...
We shall explain that for a person drawn by two simultaneous, equally powerful, and contradictory actions—like a woman being pulled by two lovers—the experience of enjoyment is impossible;
for how could enjoyment arise when there is such equality?
"When there is equality, how can enjoyment arise? [ŚBh 1.1.4]
And this being so, since in a beginningless *saṃsāra* there would be no possibility of experience for anyone at any time due to entering into such a crisis of karma,

it would follow that *saṃsāra* does not exist; therefore, to avoid this consequence, even those who do not accept God must necessarily admit the descent of the Lord’s power (*īśvara-śakti-pāta*) in this regard.
It must be accepted as being like royal power in the case of a beloved woman and so forth, because there is no other possible way [to account for it].

This repetition is intended to show that the equality of the two actions is in this very form; here, the time of the descent of power (śaktipāta) is to be understood, and not something produced by number.
The equality of the action is the time.
Commentary: For, due to the equality of their number and the absence of contradiction, there is never any impossibility of experiencing [the fruits of karma].
Otherwise, since there would be no distinction, it would follow that the descent of power (śaktipāta) occurs at all times, and consequently, the experience of karma would be impossible.
"An unexperienced karma does not perish"—this contradicts the sacred tradition (*āgama*). [Source unknown. Also cited as *śruti*.]

Therefore, because it serves as a sign of the ripening of impurity (*mala*), this "equilibrium of karma" (*karmasāmya*)—which consists in the opposition of karmic forces and is to be removed solely by the descent of power (*śaktipāta*)—is indeed distinct from what was previously described; thus there is no fault. (See *ad Mat VP* 8:103, p. 288 and following, as noted in the translation).
Now, as to what kind of those two types of karma become through the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), for that purpose [it is said]:
"Whether it be exhausted or equal.
(Vṛtti)

When all the remaining portions of both those opposing karmas have become equal through their simultaneous exhaustion, then— since no other non-exhausted karma remains to be waited for— the soul becomes extinguished along with all its constituent elements; thus, for men, there is the state of being a *vijñānakevalin* alone.
As he will say: "In that case, there is no equal enjoyment" (Kir.
The word "or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative view.
Furthermore, when it is not the case that all of the remaining portions of those two opposing karmas are equally fit for descent into the current life,

but rather that some may also exist as causes for other births and so forth, then— in accordance with that [unequal distribution]— one or the other has its power not fully descended due to the descent of power (*śaktipāta*).
Since there is no contradiction in saying "it becomes," he will state that all things indeed become objects of enjoyment;
because of the relationship between the greater and the lesser, no confusion arises.
(Quote: "Because of the relationship between the greater and the lesser, no confusion arises.")
Regarding this [verse], Kir 5:12cd], the opponent's intention is as follows: "How is that equality to be understood?"
Commentary:
How can this state of equilibrium, which consists of simultaneous mutual opposition, be attained by those two specific types of action? The meaning is that it cannot be attained at all.
The meaning is that the sequence of performance itself is required for the bestowal of the fruit.
Here, the established conclusion [is]:
how can there be a deficiency or excess of even a single *tuṭi*?
Commentary:
A *tuṭi* is a duration of time that may be either less or more. How is it perceived?
The words "by visible actions such as agriculture and so forth" are to be supplied [to the sentence].
This is what is meant: this reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because of actions such as agriculture;

for even when those [actions] are performed in sequence, it is observed that sometimes the later-performed action, having a shorter duration, quickly produces its fruit simultaneously with the previously performed one.

However, since the duration of what was previously performed is longer, it is understood that here too, such a possibility exists; thus, the equality of the two karmas is established, and there is no contradiction. Consequently, at the very moment when this subtle equality occurs, that [result] arises. (KirT 5.9)
It indeed quickly illuminates its own nature by means of the power of the mark of awakening.
Commentary:

In this way, at the very time when a similarity—consisting of mutual opposition—becomes possible for even unseen karma, just as it is for seen karma, that similarity is subtle because it is beyond the reach of people like us. At that very moment...
In due time, that power of the Supreme Lord—
which is the strength of the sign of awakening and the ripening of impurities, as it has been said:
"Having brought about the obstruction of that power, one becomes free from desire for worldly existence"— is exercised.
"Having restrained that power, one becomes free from desire for worldly existence.
This is also stated in the venerable *Mataṅga*.
With his impurities forever destroyed, he would become dispassionate toward saṃsāra.
Even when that glorious Svāyambhuva [Purāṇa] has been exhausted, there should be a desire to go toward the supreme beatitude.
(kṣīṇe tasminyiyāsā syātparaṃ niḥśreyasaṃ prati)
By that [means], he illuminates the true nature of the person—such as omniscience and so forth—by way of initiation (*dīkṣā*). As it was said by the Guru: "When one is initiated..."
"When one has been initiated by a Guru, he becomes omniscient, just like Śiva.
(Kir. 1:21bc)

The meaning is this: just as Śiva is omniscient, there is no other descent of power (*śaktipāta*) in that case which depends upon the ripening of impurity; rather, He Himself, by virtue of the context, becomes the cause for both [the removal of impurity and the descent of power]. The word *vai* (indeed) indicates another mode [of understanding], in the absence of the strength of the signs of awakening.
"Whether it be exhausted or yet incomplete," as has already been stated:
"Whether it be exhausted or yet incomplete.
(Kir. 5.9b)
Since there is another way:

thus, that descent of power (*śaktipāta*) which is heard of in other *saṃhitās* as being caused by the ripening of impurity (*malaparipāka*) is indeed declared here also to be a cause of liberation through the process of initiation (*dīkṣā*).

As for that which is heard of here as being caused by the equilibrium of karma (*karmasāmya*), it results either in the avoidance of that equilibrium or in its destruction according to the method already stated; therefore, there is no contradiction here with these particularities [found] in other *saṃhitās*.
But surely, let both of these be causes of liberation;
even so, this contradiction does not indeed arise.

Let it be so, provided there is a clear statement establishing that the equilibrium of karma (*karmasāmya*), just like the ripening of impurity (*malaparipāka*), is also a cause for that [liberation].

It has been stated that for him, the descent of power (*śaktipāta*)—which has as its fruit merely the removal of the equilibrium of karma—serves as its cause [only] in that specific context and not elsewhere; and it will be said later: "For then there is no equal experience.
(Same bhogastadā na hi).

We shall demonstrate that even in the general treatises (*sāmānyaśāstra*), it is established as having the cessation of the equality of karma (*karmasāmyanivṛtti*) as its fruit. (Kir 5:11d) [We] shall show this.
Furthermore, it is not logical that the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), which functions to remove manifest opposition, should also remove unmanifest impurities of opposition;
for since there is no distinction regarding all souls, the removal of those [impurities] would follow, resulting in the absurdity of universal liberation.

Now, it might be argued: "Just as you maintain that the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), caused by the ripening of impurity (*mala*), effects the destruction of karmas—even those whose opposition has not yet manifested—through initiation (*dīkṣā*), so too will that same [initiation] effect the destruction of impurity, even when its opposition has not yet manifested, through the cause of the equilibrium of karmas (*karmasāmya*); therefore, this undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) does not arise.
This is not so, because at that time, the fact that those [karmas] have not yet produced opposition remains unestablished.

For impurity (*mala*) is the auxiliary cause for the fruits of actions to yield their experience; without the persistence of ignorance (*avidyā*), experience would be impossible, as in the case of a liberated soul. Therefore, when that [ignorance] undergoes transformation, the actions themselves possess an emergent state of opposition [to impurity], and thus their destruction at that time is logical. However, it is not the case that there is no opposition between action and impurity while impurity remains, such that upon the cessation of the former, the latter could not persist; rather, it is because of the emergent state of opposition at that time [that action ceases].
Exhaustion might be suspected;

however, since [the power] is established as being beginningless, if one were to admit the exhaustion of even that which has not manifested its opposition, the aforementioned undesirable consequence would follow. Therefore, this descent of power (*śaktipāta*), which results solely from the removal of the contradiction regarding karma, must be accepted as threefold according to the reasoning already stated; thus, there is no contradiction.
Now, for what reason is it said that two contradictory actions can occur simultaneously?
It is because whichever portion of karma is greater first yields its fruit, while the other follows.
Commentary:
Even though a person possesses many auspicious and inauspicious karmas, that specific karma which— like agriculture and so forth— is performed later,
yet becomes superior in power due to the ripening produced by the assistance of other karmas and because of its intense momentum, [determines the result].
That very [karma] is the first to bestow its fruit;
and it has been stated by others as well that for those with intense momentum, the fruit is imminent.
As for the other [karma] besides that, it yields its fruit later, either due to the removal of some obstruction from another karma or through the recovery of its potency.
Why is this said? [It is because] when there is equality, how can enjoyment arise for one?
(Vṛtti)

This being the case, when—due to the efficacy of some cause—the two [karmas], whether both auspicious or both inauspicious, become equal through the force of their maturation or by virtue of their intense momentum, how can there be experience for that person who is drawn toward two simultaneous and contradictory actions?
It certainly does not arise; therefore, as was already stated previously, the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) must necessarily be accepted here in order to resolve this contradiction.

[Objection: But if this is so, since all actions—because they each accomplish only their own respective fruit—are equal in being mutually contradictory, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the descent of power (śaktipāta) occurs at all times.
[Reply: No, it is said.
Or if the initiating karma were mixed, then there would certainly be no equal experience [of results]. (KirT 5.11)
And something further must be stated; otherwise, there would be no experience other than pleasure.
Commentary:

For the threefold karma of a person—bestowing birth, lifespan, and experience—initiates experience; it does not merely bestow experience alone, nor does it merely bestow lifespan, because without a specific birth, experience is impossible.

Nor is it the case that [karma] which bestows birth alone [produces results], because without those two [life-span and experience], death occurs immediately after birth and experience would be impossible.

Thus, when there exists karma that bestows only experience, only life-span, or only birth—being equal [in force] yet unmixed with a heterogeneous [type]—experience would not be possible; therefore, in that case, there must be some additional heterogeneous specific karma:
one that bestows experience within [the context of] what bestows birth.

Or rather, in that case, one should state [the reason] as "because it bestows enjoyment" and so forth. Otherwise, since the experience of pleasure and pain would be impossible, even though such karma exists, he would be a *vijñānakevalin* (one liberated while still possessing consciousness); thus, there would be no consequence of the descent of grace (*śaktipāta*) occurring at all times through the contradiction of karmas, because the non-contradiction of those very karmas is always possible.
Because of the relationship between the greater and the lesser, no confusion arises.

Commentary: Even in the case of a person where two opposing actions have arisen simultaneously in equal measure, the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) does not bring about their destruction according to the principle previously stated;
rather, one becomes predominant and the other subordinate, so that no confusion or contradiction arises between them.

This very same method has been taught even in Āyurveda for the sake of avoiding confusion regarding life-prolonging and life-shortening actions: "Whether through the use of *śilājatu*, or by the grace of Śaṅkara, or through the practice of the *ajā-satra*, consumption [of karma] shall be exhausted; not otherwise. Thus it is said.
In the *Nidrāstotra* and other works, the very [prayer] spoken by Nārāyaṇabhaṭṭa is shown in the *Mahābhārata* as well: "For those exhausted in wildernesses and submerged in the great ocean...
[kāntāreṣu ca].
You are the supreme refuge for men who have been obstructed by robbers; indeed, you are the highest goal for human beings.

Even by the followers of the Sugata, in the *Tārā-stotra* and other works, [Tārā] is praised as the one who pacifies the fear of lions, elephants, fire, serpents, thieves, fetters, the great ocean, and demons:
"O you who pacify the fear of lions, elephants, fire, serpents, thieves..."
O Blessed Tārā, homage be to you!
O Blessed Tārā, who captivates with the splendor of moonbeams, homage be to you! Thus [it is said].
If that is so, how then is it born? To this he says:
"Because it is neither more nor less than emptiness, it goes to that state.
(Vṛtti)

When, for a certain person, both of those two opposing karmas become entirely equal— without any excess or deficiency— due to the disappearance of all other intervening karma, then no agitation arises; thus, because of the impossibility of any other conforming karma, the destruction of all those [opposing karmas] through the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is proclaimed.
At that time, that person whose karma has been exhausted no longer experiences that state which was previously described as "there is no enjoyment when it is equal" (Kir.
The meaning is that the purpose of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) at that time is that [the soul] attains the state of being a solitary consciousness (*vijñānakevalitva*).

Now, it is asked: "Is this descent of power—which was previously described as subtle because it is beyond the perception of those such as ourselves, or which is otherwise inferable from the cessation of disease and so forth—exactly as it was previously described, or not? It is said in reply: "That descent is to be understood as such; for his devotion is of a distinct character. (KirT 5.13)
Commentary:
That aforementioned descent of power (*śaktipāta*), which occurs at the time when the impurity has reached maturity, should be understood as residing in specific individuals;
for he in whom this occurs possesses a distinctive form of devotion (*bhakti*).
As was stated previously:
"Having brought about the restraint of its power, one becomes free from longing for existence.
(kṛtvā tacchaktisaṃrodhaṃ kriyate bhavaniḥspṛhaḥ)
In the *Śrīmatsvāyambhuva* as well, it says: "When that [knowledge] has waned, there should be the desire to go," and so forth. (Quote:
"When that has waned, there should be the desire to go.")
Then, from these two times,
that very time is proficient in the appropriation of power by itself.

Commentary: That very time for the descent of power previously mentioned is "niṣṇāta," meaning skillful; it is the "time of the grasping of the self" (ātmaparigraha) because it is therein that the self is grasped—that is, favored. That is the time.
Therefore, the Blessed One depends on that alone in that case and not on anything else;
likewise, Śiva depends on time due to the connection with beginningless karma.
That which is called "the gap in time" (kālacchidra) is the Lord Śiva, who knows it. The commentary (*vṛtti*) states:

That perfect bondage which is beginningless and consists of karma—precisely because of the impossibility of enjoyment [arising] from that, it is designated by the term "gap in time. One must take into account here that which consists of the opposition to karma.
Because the Lord knows that for those [souls], the removal of contradiction or the destruction [of karma] occurs through the descent of power (śaktipāta) and not otherwise;
therefore, it is said: why does He wait for that very time for the destruction of karmas, and not even for a time when there is no such contradiction?
Just as someone, when the target is moving, waits for a certain period of time.
Even he, Śiva, though knowing that, likewise awaits the same time.
Commentary: For just as even a bowman such as Arjuna, though extremely well-trained, does not always cut down with his own arrows the collection of weapons, such as arrows, discharged by his enemy.

However, when that which brings about injury to one's own body arises in contradiction to the life-sustaining karma (*āyuṣyakarma*), at that very moment, because of that very contradiction, the Blessed One likewise requires that same state of equilibrium characterized by the contradiction of karma during the descent of power (*śaktipāta*); for it has been stated that at that time, experience (*bhoga*) is impossible precisely because of the contradiction.

But it is not the case that even at a time when there is no contradiction, liberation occurs through non-contradiction alone, for enjoyment [of karma] is possible at that time. However, when this is not accepted, then because of the absence of equality with that [karma], there would otherwise be simultaneous liberation. (KirT 5.16)
Commentary:

Otherwise, in the absence of contradiction, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the descent of power (śaktipāta) would occur simultaneously for all persons; consequently, liberation from karma would result in the state of being a "solitary knower" (vijñānakevalitva). Therefore, to avoid this, it must necessarily be stated here that the equilibrium of karma (karmasāmya) alone is the cause; thus, there is no contradiction.

If this is so, what is the reason for saying that the Blessed One awaits a time characterized by the ripening of defilements for the sake of bestowing grace, but not also a time characterized by their non-ripening? It is said:
"If that sequence which depends upon the means of accomplishment is not accepted."
Commentary:
If that sequence of time were not required for bestowing grace, then there would be no need here for dependence upon means such as the teacher or initiation;
the consequence would be that everyone would be graced simultaneously. This is the meaning.
Therefore, there must necessarily be some cause for its removal;
and since that [removal] has been described as consisting simply in the ripening of impurities—just as cataracts and the like are removed from the eye and other organs—there is no fault whatsoever.
Now the Lord also answers the fourth question:
"Here Śiva is to be known as the Lord; however, what is considered the sovereignty of the *tuṭi*? (KirT 5.17)
Sovereignty arises from the nature of consciousness; however, one who is ignorant is not a sovereign.
Vṛtti:
As it has been stated: "Let time alone be the cause of liberation."
"What is the use of postulating Śiva here as the cause of the descent of power (śaktipāta)?
That is incorrect, because there is a difference in the nature of the cause.

For in this context, time—such as the new moon day and so forth—is the efficient cause (nimitta) because it is insentient, just like [the time for] a sacrifice; however, the Lord is the agent (kartṛ) because he is sentient, just as a twice-born man is in the case of a sacrifice on the new moon day."
Furthermore, it is not logical to claim that the consequence of the absence of an agent follows from the acceptance of a cause (*nimitta*),
because there is no contradiction between them.
However, if one accepts another [separate] agent, then that consequence indeed follows.
This very absence of contradiction regarding the effect and its agent and cause is stated by means of an illustration:
"Just as the sun possesses sovereignty over the awakening of the lotus when the time has arrived. (Kirātārjunīya 5.18)
And yet, without time, no blossoming occurs there;
nevertheless, in this world, the sun is called the awakener of the lotus.
If that fitness is also [a matter of] time, then [the word] is also figuratively expressive [of it].
Commentary:
This is stated with respect to the subject of the illustration as well.
Thus, although the timing of the action is indeed equal [for all],
nevertheless, the Lord Īśa remains here as the master of the descent of power (śaktipāta).
Commentary: Since the bound souls (*paśu*) lack the capacity— just as those who are blind and so forth cannot act as liberators from bonds—

and since the bonds themselves are insentient— just as cataracts and the like cannot spontaneously withdraw from the eyes— it is logical that He alone (the Lord) is the agent of liberation, depending upon the specific time, just as an oculist or similar physician acts for the sake of vision.
Thus, there is no fault in what has been stated.

Here, the opponent’s intention is that since the power (śakti) acts as the awakener of many persons, there arises the fault of its resulting in multiplicity; for if she is one, how can she effect the awakening of many?
The commentary states:
But according to our established doctrine, there would be no fault even if there were many [bodies], for it is not precluded by virtue of [the self's] omnipresence. (KirT 5.21)
Commentary: Since its assistance to many [entities] by virtue of its pervasiveness is not precluded,
this is therefore not a fault.
Now, the summary of the meaning of this section: Thus has the subtle conjunction of powers been explained here in this teaching.
(Vṛtti)
Thus, the descent of power (śaktipāta) has been previously described;
it has been declared by me here as being devoid of all questions.
In this context, a question arises incidentally.
Garuḍa said:
"If initiation (dīkṣā) is thus established through union with that power," [KirT 5.22]
Even after the time of initiation, concealment is observed;
if the power that effects concealment remains in him, there is no liberation.
"May that Lord act in such a way that he [the individual soul] does not become otherwise.
Commentary: Thus, by this sequence, if initiation (*dīkṣā*) for the person arises from a specific connection with the power of the Supreme Lord, then grace (*anugraha*) is the cause of liberation.

Even after the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*), because the connection with that power (*śakti*) persists, there could be no concealment (*tirobhāva*) consisting of the transgression of rules (*samaya-ullaṅghana*) and so forth. Yet such concealment is observed; therefore, since the state of being permeated by that [power] is subject to deviation, it is not established that the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is the sole cause of grace (*anugraha*). As it has been said:
"When one is initiated by a Guru through the intense descent of power..."
Furthermore, this statement— "When one is initiated by a Guru through the descent of intense power" (Kirana Tantra 1.21ab)— is likewise untenable.

Now, if it is argued that this [descent of power] has grace as its cause, then let him act accordingly; for he is the "Lord" (svāmī) because he possesses his own power (śakti-pāta). The meaning is that this Person should not otherwise engage in the causes of concealment (*tirobhāva*).

However, he does not act in such a way, since at that time we observe the performance of the very causes of concealment; therefore, the descent of power is not the cause of grace—this is the prima facie argument (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
On this point, the Blessed One stated the established conclusion: "By the will of Śiva, that [power] belongs to those persons who have attained concealment. (KirT 5.24)
She is not called *tirohikā* because she effects concealment;
for she does not cause a fall into concealment, since her nature is characterized by grace.
Commentary:

Here, the connection is as follows: first of all, for those who have entered into concealment (*tirobhāva*) and whose impurities (*mala*) are not yet transformed, that [gracious] power does not remain as a bestower of grace;
nor has initiation (*dīkṣā*) been performed for them by teachers out of greed, ignorance, and so forth, because it is stated that such [initiation] exists only by the will of Śiva.
Since knowledge is not possible for her, that [initiation] is indeed fruitless for those who lack qualification, such as Śūdras, just like the *upanayana* and other rites.
However, it is said that at that time, another concealing power (*tirodhikā śakti*) remains for them as the agent of concealment;
for, as has been stated, a descent [of grace] for the sake of concealment is impossible for her, because she possesses the nature of bestowing grace (*anugraha*).
If the power that causes concealment remains within him, there is no liberation for him.
This point, for its part, remains unproven.
If this is so, then since [the Lord] has the nature of bestowing grace, why does he not ordain grace for all? To this, it is replied:
By that [cause] through which the time is most imminent, by that He reveals Himself.
*Vṛtti*:
It has been stated that for whatever reason, for whichever person the time for the ripening of impurity (*mala*) is imminent, for that very person He reveals Himself.
"Having restrained that power, one acts free from desire for existence.
(Kir. 2.29cd)
Therefore, this objection is also without fault.
As for what was said—that even after initiation, how can that power remain as a cause of concealment—that too is incorrect; because:
Having manifested itself like a flash of lightning, that power which awakens the person departs.
Commentary:
Having then brought about for the person an awakening consisting of the destruction of impurity, that power, like a flash of lightning, departs after a very short time and ceases from that activity.
The sense is that this matter is established by logic itself, based on the principle that what has already been accomplished cannot be accomplished again.

However, as for the attainment of liberation following initiation (*dīkṣā*), that [liberation] remains generally present by virtue of [the Lord’s] presiding over it; thus, there is no fault of deviation regarding the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) with respect to grace.
Even so, there is the fault of the consequence of initiation deviating from liberation, because one observes its concealment at a subsequent time. To this, it is replied:
If this [individual], though initiated, were concealed in every respect, then even in both types of concealment, the attainment of a [higher] station might occur somewhere. (KirT 5.27)
Commentary:
It has been stated that although one who has not been initiated is concealed from all perspectives, once he has received initiation, he is [no longer so].
Even if this person, despite being properly initiated, should at some time become concealed from all perspectives due to an obstacle—whether divine or human—[the following applies].

Because of the word "or" (*vā*), even when this [power] is concealed in these two ways— not in its entirety and not at all— there occurs, in some cases, namely in certain instances such as with carnivorous animals and the like, the attainment of the fruit of transgressing the rules (*samaya*).
As it is said in the venerable *Pauṣkara*:
"Because of the transgression of the samaya, it is declared that one becomes a flesh-eater for a hundred years. [Source not traced]
Pau, but = /Sar/ 25:2cd. Cf. note ad *KirV* 1:10.5.
That same half-verse is quoted there and in 6:8.12.
However, the word "in some cases" (kvacit) is used because [the transgression] is not necessarily exhausted by the penances to be described for every violation of the rules. What follows from this?
It is said: for one who remains in that state, only that very latent impression (vāsanā) arises here.
For one who is thus engaged, there arises the non-conceptual liberation of the self.
Commentary:

In that regard, even for an initiated person who has transgressed the rules (*samaya*) and is situated in the body of a flesh-eater (*kravyāda*), such as a *piśāca* or similar being, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) remains the very same.
That very impression which was observed to be the cause of devotion to Śiva and so forth among those who have not transgressed the rules is what becomes manifest.

Therefore, due to the connection with the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of having been initiated, one experiences the fruit of that [transgression] as a hindrance to the fruit of initiation—just like a fruit of desire—and having experienced it, this self certainly attains liberation, which is the fruit of initiation. As it has been said:
"The destiny of one purified by expiation is proclaimed to be pure. (Prāyaścittaviśuddhasya gatiḥ śuddhā prakīrtitā).
Source unknown.
For in this manner,
through this sequential yoga, one may become concealed.
There would be the consequence of futility if that liberation were not to exist.
Commentary:

By this sequential process—first the ripening of impurity (*malaparipāka*), then the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), and then initiation (*dīkṣā*)—one who has been initiated might somehow fall into concealment (*tirobhāva*).

If, after that, due to the experience of the fruit resulting from the transgression of rules (*samayātikrama*), liberation (*mukti*)—which is the fruit of that initiation—does not occur, [then what follows?]
Consequently, the sequence of that initiation would result in being purposeless.

Nor can it be argued that this [purposelessness] is justified because it is the activity of the Supreme Lord; rather, one must necessarily admit that his liberation occurs at that very moment from that [descent of power] alone. Thus, there is no fault of the initiation itself resulting in a deviation from its own function. Now, if the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) or the connection with initiation is equal for all, why is it that only some person, at a later time, becomes joined with concealment (*tirobhāva*) while another does not? To this it is replied:
The power [of the latent impression] is dull or very dull, due to the intention to express the equilibrium of karma.
Commentary:

Because the intention to express—that is, the dullness or extreme dullness—which constitutes the equilibrium of karma characterized by the ripening of impurities (*mala*), serves as the cause for that intention, it is called "intention" (*vivakṣā*).

Indeed, for one who is approached by that [power] acting as a cause— whether it be the Lord’s power (*śakti*) characterized as dull or very dull, or initiation (*dīkṣā*)— there certainly occurs a connection with transgression (*pratyavāya*).

However, for one whose karma is characterized by the ripening of impurity (*mala*) and is intense or very intense, such that the power falls upon him as intense or very intense according to that [degree of karma], there is no transgression whatsoever.
It is said that [the result] arises.
Thus, by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), the status of being a cause for transgression (*pratyavāya*) should be understood as resulting from the weakness of the power of grace;
it is not otherwise. So it is stated.
Furthermore, such a power is not subject to transformation like milk.
For the power of the possessor of power manifests as the distinctions of functions and forms;
and that ladder of castes, beginning with the twice-born, clearly brings about liberation.
Commentary:

Furthermore, it is not logically tenable that the very power of grace (*anugraha-śakti*) undergoes the state of concealment (*tirobhāva*); for it has been stated that the power of the Supreme Lord attains differentiation only through the specific arrangement—that is, the persistence (*sthiti*)—of its respective function, and not in a primary sense.
Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śānta are distinguished according to the difference in their functions. (Kiraṇa-tantra 3.13cd)
And therefore, like the Supreme Lord, the *vatsā* (the offspring) is also indeed non-transforming; as it has been said:
"Transformation is not possible for the conscious, nor for the unconscious. (pariṇāmo 'cetanasya cetanasya na yujyate).

And that [initiation] is a ladder— a series of steps— for the twice-born and other castes who are proceeding toward the supreme state known as liberation, because it is the cause of upward movement. Thus,
when one has been initiated by a Guru through the descent of the intense power (tīvra-śakti-nipāta)...
"The moment one is initiated by a Guru through the descent of intense power" (Kirana Tantra 1.21ab)— this very statement is indeed well-spoken.
Thus ends the fifth chapter.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmatkiraṇa composed by Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha, the son of Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha.
Then, for the purpose of examining the category of *upāya*, Garuḍa spoke another section in the form of a question:
"Śiva, the supreme cause, has been declared to be the benefactor of all."
But those twice-born castes who exist in states of deficiency or excess [of qualities], // KirT_6.1 //

If the formative impression (*saṃskāra*) were likewise [to produce its effect], why would the fruit not be likewise? How could there be a variation in degree—lesser or greater—among those [fruits] if the formative impression were identical to them? (KirT 6.2)
Commentary: Here, the word-meanings, the context, and the connection [of this sūtra] should be understood as before.
However, that which consists of sentences is of many kinds, such as "the one initiated by the Guru" (guruṇā dīkṣitaḥ) and so forth.
Since it was already shown at the very conclusion of the preceding chapter that [the initiate] has been initiated by the Guru (Kir. 1.21b), [the details thereof need not be repeated here].

And this is the meaning of the question here: it has been stated that the Supreme Lord, following the ripening of impurity (*mala*), is the apprehender (*grāhaka*) of all [beings] by virtue of being their object of refinement (*saṃskārya*).
Among these, however, there are three twice-born castes (*dvijāti-varṇa*), not just one. As it has been said:

"The first birth is from the mother; the other is that which pertains to the initiation ceremony (*aupanāyanika*). Because of this [latter], the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are called 'twice-born' (*dvijāti*). Thus it is said.
(Quotation: "The first [birth] is from the mother...")
Thus it was said by him to those twice-born ones:
"By the very nature of their birth, like cows, gavayas, donkeys, and so forth, they abide in the general scriptures according to superior, middling, and inferior [capacities]."

Furthermore, that sacrament (saṃskāra) prescribed by the general scriptures— consisting of forty-eight varieties beginning with *garbhādhāna*— is held by those learned in the Vedas to have as its fruit merely the removal of the state of being fallen (*patitatva*) for that [person's] caste, or for his body.
As Manu has said:

"The purifying refinement of the body must be performed, both for the sake of this world and the next, by means of the rites pertaining to the womb, the fire-oblations, the birth-rite, the tonsure, and the tying of the girdle. Thus it is said.
"The refinement of the body must be performed."

And therefore, this [rite] called initiation (*dīkṣā*), being a *saṃskāra*, must belong either to the caste (*jāti*) or to the body, because it is a *saṃskāra*— just like the tying of the girdle (*mauñjīnibandhana*), as stated in Manusmṛti 2.26.
And likewise, why would its fruit not be of the nature of grace in that very same way?
It would be nothing at all. And therefore, when one has been initiated by a Guru...
Just as that Śiva is omniscient, so too is he who has been initiated by the Guru.
The meaning is that there is a contradiction with this scriptural passage [Kir 1:21bc].
For since this refinement (saṃskāra) is similar to theirs according to the Veda, how can it be that their destiny is inferior to that of the Vedic [path] and superior to that of this [worldly path]?
The question is: "It is simply not possible.
But as for the established conclusion, the Blessed One said:
The refinement of a living being is considered to belong neither to its birth nor to its body.
Commentary:
This refinement is held to pertain neither to the genus nor to the physical body.
Rather, because of the scriptural statement that it consists of favoring sentient beings alone, one should not conceive of it otherwise based merely on its similarity [to other things].
Therefore, this is not a fault.

However, as for those who imagine that this [rite], being a refinement (*saṃskāra*), will benefit the person through its very visible form—just as the *śrāddha* and other rites benefit the father, grandfather, and so forth by means of the refinement of the lineage (*jāti*) or of the body—they [are mistaken].
If it were due to birth, then when one person has been initiated, everyone would be initiated.
Therefore, it is not said that [Śiva] is born from [the body], for he is considered to be insentient by nature;
rather, Śiva is declared to be the benefactor of all, bestowing grace upon the form of consciousness.

Commentary: Since the universal (jāti) resides in all persons without distinction, if a refinement (saṃskāra) were performed for the sake of the liberation of one person, it would follow that all persons would be liberated.

Although this consequence does not apply to the body because the body differs according to the difference between persons, any refinement of it is declared to be entirely fruitless due to its insentience (jaḍatva).
Now, if it is said that this impression belongs to consciousness alone by way of that [object], then there is no contradiction,
since we have already stated that it is an assistance to the nature of consciousness.
Regarding this very point, a question is raised for the sake of further investigation:
Garuḍa said:
"O Lord, because you are the bestower of grace upon all—even upon children, the ignorant, and serpents—you must extend that grace;
and it must be preceded by the performance of purificatory rites."
When it is stated in the Tantra that liberation occurs through ritual action alone, then practices such as ritual performance, knowledge, and vows are not the cause [of liberation]. (KirT 6.6)
Commentary: For here, the Supreme Lord is the grasper of all [souls] after the ripening of their impurities (*mala*), as they are to be purified;
from among them—
"One shall be a child until the sixteenth [year]."
In *Mṛgāṅkavṛtti* on *Vākyapadīya* 10:14, pp.
266–7, and on *Maṭhara-vṛtti* on *Vākyapadīya* 12:5c–6c, p. 339, Bhaṭṭa observes that it appears (with some...)
differences) in the *Śabdakalpadruma* (s.v.
*bāla*) attributed to Bharata.
According to this traditional teaching (*smṛti*), a "child" (*bāla*) is said to be one who has not yet reached the time for practicing the study of grammar, logic, and the scriptures.

However, a "fool" (*bāliśa*) is not merely one who is younger than that; because he lacks the certainty of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) and thus possesses no personal qualification (*anadhikāritva*), he is indeed unfit for consecration (*asaṃskārya*).
Rather, like women, *śūdras*, and others, he is called a fool because he is incapable of hearing the scriptures on grammar, logic, and epistemology, just like a child.
Furthermore, the enjoyer (*bhogī*) is not one who is solely intent upon enjoyment;
because he lacks the ripening of impurities (*mala*), he has no further obligation toward formative impressions (*saṃskāra*). As it is said:
"Having restrained that power, one becomes free from longing for worldly existence."
"Having restrained that power, one becomes free from longing for existence.
Thus also said the illustrious Vidyādhipati.
Surely those who still have a longing for enjoyment—which is the very cause of worldly existence—have not been appointed by your power;
for how could they have crossed to the far shore of the terrifying great ocean when their bodies were being devoured by sea-monsters while crossing?
(te tvacchaktyā...)
Those whose bodies have been devoured by aquatic creatures cross over [the waters].
These [three verses] are likely from the lost *Mānastotra*, three of which are quoted in *Tantrāloka* 14:10–12.
These are also in the *mattamayūra* metre and possess a similar rhetorical structure. (A *vidyādhipati* is also cited ad *Mokṣa* 69.)

Rather, it refers specifically to kings and others who, though possessing the scriptures consisting of heard words and sentences and having reached the time for their practice, have failed to perform that practice due to the distractions of worldly power.

When the impurity of these individuals has reached its full maturation, the Supreme Lord must necessarily bestow grace, which consists of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). And the meaning is that such grace is precisely the previously mentioned cause for the purification (*saṃskāra*) that constitutes initiation (*dīkṣā*). Consequently...
"When one is initiated by a guru through the intense descent of power, he becomes omniscient, just like Śiva. (ŚDV 1.29)
Just as Śiva is omniscient,
so too [is he] through the Veda, the Āgama, and purification alone, like that of a child and others.

The question is as follows: "If it is declared that liberation belongs to everyone, then our own knowledge and other qualities—which were stated to be practices to be performed after initiation—would be rendered useless; for even here, since liberation is established through mere consecration (*saṃskāra*) for children and others who are unfit for knowledge and so forth due to their lack of refinement in the rules of grammar, logic, and epistemology, this performance of ritual action, knowledge, and the like would not be a means to the human goal for us either, and thus it should not be performed. This is the objection.
As for the established conclusion,
the Blessed One said:
"O Tārkṣya, the Lord bestows grace exactly upon those who abide in whatever state they are."
Commentary:

The meaning is that the Blessed One, by examining the ripening of their impurities, bestows grace upon all of them—both those established through the refinement of words, sentences, and so forth, and others such as children who follow different methods—and he does not abandon those who are unfit for knowledge. For it is thus:
And some among them are capable of action; their liberation is likewise.
Likewise, some are fit for knowledge, while others are fit for conduct;
thus, for those to whom liberation has been proclaimed, it occurs through union with the Lord.

Commentary: Among those for whom liberation, characterized as the state of Sadāśiva, has been described in the very section on initiation (*dīkṣāprakaraṇa*), some here— namely the *bāla*s and the *bhogin*s— are fit for ritual action (*kriyā*) consisting of sacrifice (*yāga*) which is external to recitation (*japa*) and distinct from the mental [recitation], but not for knowledge (*jñāna*).
But surely, without knowledge, even the capacity for action is not possible; as they say:
"And having known, one performs [the rite].
(jñātvā cānuṣṭhānam)
Source unknown. Cf. Jayaratha on *Tantrāloka* 15.11:
"The intention is that once [the truth] is known, there will be practice;
this is true. However, because that [practice] is necessitated by action, such knowledge has as its object only a single portion of the scripture."
Since it has been stated that action alone [is required], there is no contradiction.

However, those others who are proficient in words, sentences, and the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)—distinct from those previously mentioned—are authorized as teachers (*ācāryas*) because they are fit for knowledge, exposition, and the investigation of their meaning.
On the other hand, those others who, due to their childishness, are unfit even for action are [authorized] only for conduct (*caryā*) consisting of vows such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*.

Because they are qualified, they are authorized; thus, by the Lord’s injunction following initiation, for those who are entitled to ritual action, knowledge, and so forth, liberation has been declared—along with the results of transgressions—in accordance with the manner of performing obligatory and occasional rites. It must be understood that these [rites] are to be performed by them in exactly that way. Otherwise...
"Because of the transgression of the *samaya*, it is said that one becomes a flesh-eater for a hundred years. (Sarvācāra-tantra 25.2cd;
cf. Kiraṇa-vṛtti 5.27.6 and 1.10.5).
The meaning of the footnote to the translation of the latter is that their liberation does not consist in [attaining] fruits that result in transgression.

Thus, first of all, the objection regarding the necessity of performing all [prescribed acts] has been refuted on the grounds that knowledge and the other [means] are enjoined according to one's specific qualification (*adhikāra*).
As for what was asked—"For what purpose are these practices performed?"—it is said in response:
"Initiation (dīkṣā) is held to be the cause of the means, such as knowledge and the rest;
liberation does not occur through initiation alone, for it is that [initiation] which is the regulating means. (KirT 6.9)
Commentary: It is not the case that knowledge and the other [means] are purposeless here, because they are heard of in scripture as being the means.

However, since they are heard of in scripture as being preceded by initiation (*dīkṣā*), liberation from bondage—which would otherwise be the effect—is not brought about by them alone, for it is not accomplished by those [means] without that [initiation].

Moreover, that means (upāya) is a regulator (*niyāmaka*); for those [fetters] for whom a restrictive rule (*niyama*) consisting of severance has not been performed by initiation (*dīkṣā*) for the sake of liberation from their bonds, that means—consisting of knowledge and so forth—is said to be the regulator, the cause of severance, for only some of them. For it is said: "Those means are proclaimed as such because they effect the favor of all."
Why was only one means not taught by him, since it is otherwise?
Commentary:

For here, by means of the initiation for immediate liberation (*asadyonirvāṇadīk�śā*), which—according to the reasoning to be stated—prevents the experience of the fruits of karma already set in motion;
quote: {by the reasoning to be stated...}
*Kir* 6:20 and commentary:

Even that grace (*anugraha*), which consists in the manifestation of Śiva-nature through the total severance of impurity (*mala*) and so forth, which has not yet been performed by the Lord, must likewise be accomplished by Him through the means of instruction.

Therefore, when only that much remains to be completed through initiation (*dīkṣā*)—namely, the severance of impurity and the like—those means such as knowledge (*jñāna*) and the rest are proclaimed [as necessary].

By those means, the cessation of impurities (*mala*) and the like, as well as the manifestation of one's *śivatva* (divine nature), must be accomplished by the initiates (*dīkṣita*) gradually day by day, in such a way that no contradiction arises with the karma whose effects have already begun (*ārabdhakārya*).

Nor should there be a dependence on any other cause for the subsequent cessation of such bondage and the manifestation of *śivatva*. If this were not the intention of the Supreme Lord (*Parameśvara*), then why would He have taught only a single means called initiation (*dīkṣā*)?

Once the accomplishment of the purpose has arisen, how could there be the persistence of the body?

Therefore, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the scriptural statement regarding the destruction of all bonds through initiation (*dīkṣā*) is not authoritative, because it is sublated by perception and other means of knowledge, just like the scriptural statement "one should sprinkle with fire.

Just as the spinning of the wheel is for the purpose of producing a jar, and even when that [production] has occurred— that is, once it is accomplished— the spinning of the wheel is still seen to continue solely due to its residual momentum (*saṃskāra*), so too, in the initiation of immediate liberation (*sadyonirvāṇadīkṣā*), although all bonds such as karma have been destroyed, [the body continues] solely due to their residual momentum.

"The fault of the body's falling [into pieces] occurs immediately after initiation.

Thus, because the scriptural statement regarding the fruit of initiation (*dīkṣā*) is sublated by another means of knowledge, it lacks authority; such is the meaning of the question.

The Blessed One said:
"The sign of that [state] is the culmination of latent impressions and non-conceptuality regarding those actions.

This is the meaning: it has been stated that in the initiation for immediate liberation (*asadyonirvāṇadīkṣā*), the karma that bestows experience upon this present body is not to be destroyed for the person.

Since experience is impossible without impurity (*mala*) and the causal instruments (*kāryakaraṇa*), it follows that there is no total severance of impurity and the subtle body; rather, there is a severance only in part, by way of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*), which obstructs those experiences. For in that case, since the severance of other bonds is also not established in its entirety, the manifestation of Śiva-nature is impossible; therefore, the signs thereof—such as omniscience and so forth—[are not yet fully realized].
The word "is not seen" is to be supplied [to the sentence]. This is because the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of impurities and so forth do exist.
As for the statement that no other sign of it is perceived either, that is incorrect, because by this [reasoning], these two—the impurity and the sign—[are established].
It has been stated that *vāsanā* consists merely of the residual portion remaining after initiation (*dīkṣā*). Its culmination is its final destruction.

For that purpose, there is the absence of conceptualization (*avikalpanā*)—the non-existence of conceptual thought—regarding those obligatory, occasional, and non-prohibited rites consisting of knowledge, action, and conduct that were previously explained.
This discernment in performing them exactly as prescribed is indeed seen to be the infallible sign of liberation from the fetters (*pāśa*), even at this stage.

Commentary:

When it is argued that because the self is all-pervasive (*vibhutva*), its apprehension is not possible— and this is the meaning of the reason— then how is this pervasive nature of the self inferred and grasped through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) and through knowledge, yoga, and so forth, as being "situated in the body" (*tanustha*), that is, manifested by means of the body and the instruments [of perception]?
The meaning is that because [the self] is conditioned (*saṃskriyate*), this reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Likewise, since [the self] is inferred and apprehended through vibration (*parispanda*) in another body—just as in its own body—by means of signs such as the activities of body and speech, it is therefore also inconclusive. It is stated that this is also the case with space (*ākāśa*).
Just as space is pervasive, and just as the formless poison is apprehended through the power of a mantra, so too is this quality,
which possesses that same power, to be expressed.

Since space was previously described as an effect, its omnipresence (*vibhutva*) is impossible; therefore, although it is more extensive than other elements here, it is perceived by means of its specific quality, which is sound in nature, and is accepted as such by yogis.
In the same way, in this scripture, the disciple is grasped through the power of the mantra.
Since the state of being susceptible to refinement (*saṃskāryatva*) is possible, there is no logical inconsistency in the application [of the mantra].

As for what was also said— that because the subtle body is formless and, due to the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), beyond the perception of people such as ourselves, it cannot be grasped by the initiated even through that medium—

Just as that power of killing, denoted by the word "poison," is grasped by people such as ourselves, so too is that which is denoted by the word "Self," consisting of knowledge and action.

Furthermore, the *guṇa* (attribute), which is denoted by the very term "subtle body" (*sūkṣmadeha*) and consists of the instruments of experience, is grasped and refined through the power of the mantra according to the scriptures; thus, there is no defect here regarding the impossibility of refinement due to a lack of logical connection.
